quoted_text:
We are terminating Chris Degnan for unethical conduct involving Cognition.

The last few months have seen incredible progress in AI capabilities. San Francisco has flourished as new companies that solve new, more ambitious problems are finding great success. Generally, it is a wonderful time to be building.

We at @FactoryAI have seen overwhelming interest in our model-agnostic coding agents and our software factory product. Our team has 10x’d in size, while our revenue has 100x’d year over year. This momentum has been unprecedented.

A much larger competitor, Cognition (makers of Devin) has fallen behind us on the capabilities that matter most to customers: cost, quality, and security. Instead of competing in the market, Cognition engineers feigned interviews with us to pry information about our product. Not finding what they were looking for, Cognition has decided to throw their weight and money at people with direct knowledge of our most confidential plans.

It feels as though ethics is being thrown out of the window in the AI era. People are willing to do anything, including exploiting privileged information and violating ethical boundaries. I think this is unique to our time, and I don’t think it’s right. Integrity still matters.

Yesterday, I made the decision to immediately terminate Christopher Degnan’s roles as a Board Observer and Advisor to Factory, after over a year of service.

Prior to this decision, Chris told me he had a casual conversation with an executive at Cognition AI. When I questioned his intentions, he reassured me that ethics aside, he had “made too much money” and was “too lazy to go work for Cognition,” which I trusted and believed.

On Monday, Chris spent time advising the Factory team on a handful of confidential board-level matters. That evening, he called me to say that the conversation that was initially described as casual and one-off was actually formal and recurring. For weeks, while he sat in our board meetings and advised our leadership team, he was also confiding with executives of our largest competitor. Chris was subject to confidentiality obligations in connection with his work with Factory. We do not know the extent of the information he shared, but it puts his timely questions about our product roadmap and what the parity gap involves into a new light.

It is sad to sever a relationship with someone who has been a trusted advisor - and even a close friend -  for over a year. But Chris’s conduct is unacceptable to me. Trust in Board Membership is one of the sacred bonds in the Silicon Valley, one that helps the startup ecosystem thrive. With it comes an enormous responsibility. That trust was violated.

Competition is good. I respect and in many cases admire our competitors. San Francisco is a beautiful, singular place where the bold and ambitious go to defy the norms and precedents of the past. But certain principles that must remain. Violating ethics to seek advantage turns what should be positive-sum into zero-sum.

We all love technology. And we all love to compete. But we must hold ourselves to a higher standard. The future of software engineering comes with abundance that will impact every person on Earth. Building that future comes with immense responsibility. We must build and compete with integrity.

quoted_text:
I think Crypto VC is coming to an end for a multitude of reasons.

First of all, no offence, but VCs are pretty useless anyway. 

They used to provide brand value, but today that matters much less than ever before.

Contrary to common perception, in my experience the public provides as much signal, if not more than VCs. And venture capital is just as narrative chasing as degens on fomo, the difference is that public markets are more generous and willing.

One big advantage of the public is that they don’t care at all about competition with their existing bags. VCs have illiquid portcos that skew their bias, the public couldn’t care less about competition. 

They’ll invest in two competing products because… why not both?

VCs also tend to slopify everything they touch. As soon as you’re raising from venture capital, you automatically revert to mean. You become average. 

And if an idea is truly interesting, VCs will strip away any notion of “being early,” which is a concept that attracts many ppl to crypto in the first place. 

Remember democratizing access? That’s a pillar of this industry.

For founders, it’s far better to raise from the public and give that upside to a large community instead of concentrating it to a couple funds, because if you succeed, you’ll benefit from a massive self-marketing machine.

No better advertising than making your community some money. 

That last point is under rated, it’s something that VC only projects simply cannot match, regardless of any airdrop or whatever else.

When someone believes in something, puts money behind it, then gets rewarded, they feel like absolute champs. They will love the project even long after they sell.

No VC funded airdrop farm will create that same level of organic support.

Lastly, regulations used to heavily favor VCs, but now that the climate is changing, the VC edge is disintegrating.

So yeah, I agree that crypto VC is on its last breath, and I think that a large part of it is because they’re becoming unnecessary.

author: a16z
quoted_text:
a16z's David George, Sarah Wang, Alex Immerman, and Santiago Rodriguez on the State of Markets, from AI and infrastructure to the next investment cycles:

1. Tech is the everything cycle.

High-tech equipment, software, and R&D are now about 55% of US capital spending, and the AI buildout just passed the railroads as a share of GDP. The five largest hyperscalers will spend about $780B on capex this year, heading past $1T in 2027, and demand still outstrips supply at every point in the chain.

2. It's an earnings story.

Stocks are up about 20% while multiples are down about 20%, and the S&P trades under 20x earnings. The market is up 90% since ChatGPT, on 15% earnings growth.

3. AI adoption is broad and shallow.

69% of the S&P 500 has a live AI deployment, 30% report a quantified result, and just 2% have AI doing a job they'd notice if it stopped. The power users are pulling away: the top 1% of AI spenders spend eight times the top 10%.

4. The private markets are enormous.

Six private companies, Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, and Revolut, add up to about $2.4T by last round, more than every IPO of the past decade combined. "The founder is the asset class. The IPO is another financing event."

Plus: why a data center can lower your electricity bill, what Amazon saying no to Muse and Instacart saying yes tells you about marketplaces, and the seven areas the team is most excited about next.

text:
CBS News and Kalshi are partnering for the midterms.

Kalshi forecasts for key races and control of Congress will complement CBS’s reporting, polling, and expert analysis.

Markets aggregate beliefs from millions of Americans and force ideas from all sides to compete in the open, driven by a simple and transparent incentive: to be right.

They give someone who spots a mistaken consensus a financial incentive to challenge it: if you think the market has it wrong, you can trade against it and be rewarded. You basically get paid to be right. That opportunity gives people a reason to dig deeper, build better models, find information others missed, and challenge assumptions others take for granted by trading on the knowledge they acquired.

Their competing views and collective knowledge become a public forecast that updates in real-time and that we all benefit from, whether we ever place a trade or not.

Unlike most sources of information, this information is produced bottom-up, not by elites, but by millions of people researching and trading across the country.

And now CBS viewers will have access to it.

text:
We are terminating Chris Degnan for unethical conduct involving Cognition.

The last few months have seen incredible progress in AI capabilities. San Francisco has flourished as new companies that solve new, more ambitious problems are finding great success. Generally, it is a wonderful time to be building.

We at @FactoryAI have seen overwhelming interest in our model-agnostic coding agents and our software factory product. Our team has 10x’d in size, while our revenue has 100x’d year over year. This momentum has been unprecedented.

A much larger competitor, Cognition (makers of Devin) has fallen behind us on the capabilities that matter most to customers: cost, quality, and security. Instead of competing in the market, Cognition engineers feigned interviews with us to pry information about our product. Not finding what they were looking for, Cognition has decided to throw their weight and money at people with direct knowledge of our most confidential plans.

It feels as though ethics is being thrown out of the window in the AI era. People are willing to do anything, including exploiting privileged information and violating ethical boundaries. I think this is unique to our time, and I don’t think it’s right. Integrity still matters.

Yesterday, I made the decision to immediately terminate Christopher Degnan’s roles as a Board Observer and Advisor to Factory, after over a year of service.

Prior to this decision, Chris told me he had a casual conversation with an executive at Cognition AI. When I questioned his intentions, he reassured me that ethics aside, he had “made too much money” and was “too lazy to go work for Cognition,” which I trusted and believed.

On Monday, Chris spent time advising the Factory team on a handful of confidential board-level matters. That evening, he called me to say that the conversation that was initially described as casual and one-off was actually formal and recurring. For weeks, while he sat in our board meetings and advised our leadership team, he was also confiding with executives of our largest competitor. Chris was subject to confidentiality obligations in connection with his work with Factory. We do not know the extent of the information he shared, but it puts his timely questions about our product roadmap and what the parity gap involves into a new light.

It is sad to sever a relationship with someone who has been a trusted advisor - and even a close friend -  for over a year. But Chris’s conduct is unacceptable to me. Trust in Board Membership is one of the sacred bonds in the Silicon Valley, one that helps the startup ecosystem thrive. With it comes an enormous responsibility. That trust was violated.

Competition is good. I respect and in many cases admire our competitors. San Francisco is a beautiful, singular place where the bold and ambitious go to defy the norms and precedents of the past. But certain principles that must remain. Violating ethics to seek advantage turns what should be positive-sum into zero-sum.

We all love technology. And we all love to compete. But we must hold ourselves to a higher standard. The future of software engineering comes with abundance that will impact every person on Earth. Building that future comes with immense responsibility. We must build and compete with integrity.

quoted_text:
The #1 life hack to becoming more productive, to becoming respected & trusted by everyone you work with:

Responding to every message within seconds or minutes and rarely hours.

It is no secret that the world's busiest and most successful people are also the fastest to respond.

But how does one become hyper responsive?

You adopt a rigorous strategy across all of your messaging surfaces. The goal is to eliminate overall noise, and never have a large pileup of messages such that the mental overhang of responding becomes a problem.

Here is my comprehensive personal messaging strategy that I’ve employed in some fashion for over 20 years to be the most responsive person you know.

First, some global rules:

1. You will process but not respond to most messages by phone. You will respond to most on your laptop. Why? Touch interface is fast for organizing but keyboard is better for writing.

2. Turn off all group notifications on all apps, on deskop and mobile. Leave unread badges on, and leave notifications on for DMs.

3. You cannot adopt inbox zero progressively. You must simply declare messaging bankruptcy and start from scratch. How? MARK AS READ for all messaging apps, ARCHIVE ALL for email. You won't miss anything I promise.

4. You do not use folders in any app. They will no longer be useful when you have no messaging debt.

5. You aren’t deleting. You are using unread/read as replacements for unfinished/finished. The only place where we remove messages is email (archive to preserve search).

Now, app by app strategies:

iMessage/Signal:

Always first priority, read & respond instantly. Priority not because high signal but because you can’t apply any inbox mgmt strategies.

Email:

1. Your inbox is a todo list

2. Read all emails as they come in (but don't reply)

3. Archive anything you don’t need to respond to
4. Use "skip it and archive" filtering for frequent messages (in Gmail, search bar for sender or subject, create a filter rule)

5. Unsubscribe from every newsletter as it comes in. If this isn’t working, you can create a filter. But you need to progressively eliminate spam as a high priority

6. When ready to reply on desktop, hit archive. Keep your inbox clean

Slack:

1. In order to clear: click groups with no mentions but don’t read, read & respond to groups with mentions

2.  Mute all groups with > 20, you can read on a Saturday if you want

3. Unread DMs, long hold and preview before reading. If easy, respond on phone. If not, leave and respond at desktop

Telegram/Whatsapp:

1. Two folders, Unread, and All

2. Mute all groups

3. In order: click in and out of groups with no mentions, then read and respond to groups with mentions

4. Handle DMs last, long hold and preview first. If instant, respond on phone. If not, leave and respond later.

5. Leave groups aggressively, don’t join any channels or social chats > 20 people. If you find yourself in one, leave.

X/LinkedIn/Instagram/etc.

1. Allow message requests from verified users

2. A lot of spam but can apply read/unread strategy

3. Read all to get started

I know this is lengthy but once you get the basics, you will build a new mental model of how to deal with messages from everywhere.

And you will soon have empty inboxes everywhere, allowing you to reply to new ones with tremendous speed.

author: AlphaSeeker21
quoted_text:
SEAL is fully shipped. $ANYR 

Anyroute SEAL is private, verifiable infrastructure for open and uncensored models.

It is built around four parts:

S: Sidecar  
The model runs behind an attested Sidecar. The hardware proves the environment, the model weights are measured, keys are created inside the enclave, and every response can be tied back to that record.

E: Encrypted transport  
Your request is encrypted to the enclave. A relay separates your IP from the request path, so the operator handling the model does not need to know who sent it.

A: Anonymous credits  
Payment and prompting are separated. Blind credits let a request be paid for without attaching the payer’s identity to the prompt or the receipt.

L: Ledger of receipts  
Every response returns a signed receipt. It records the model, route, attestation, policy, and hashes of the request and response, not the content itself. Streams are hash-chained, so altered or cut output can be detected. Receipt records are anchored on-chain for verification.

SEAL also makes policy visible. If filtering is enabled, the policy is measured inside the enclave and named in the receipt. No hidden changes after the fact.

Builders can use it with OpenAI-compatible model servers, Claude Code, Codex, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Saved Routes, Batch Studio, and private RAG.

The point is not to ask users to trust a privacy policy.

The point is to show what ran, where the request went, what was retained, who could see what, and give the user a receipt they can verify themselves.

quoted_text:
The #1 life hack to becoming more productive, to becoming respected & trusted by everyone you work with:

Responding to every message within seconds or minutes and rarely hours.

It is no secret that the world's busiest and most successful people are also the fastest to respond.

But how does one become hyper responsive?

You adopt a rigorous strategy across all of your messaging surfaces. The goal is to eliminate overall noise, and never have a large pileup of messages such that the mental overhang of responding becomes a problem.

Here is my comprehensive personal messaging strategy that I’ve employed in some fashion for over 20 years to be the most responsive person you know.

First, some global rules:

1. You will process but not respond to most messages by phone. You will respond to most on your laptop. Why? Touch interface is fast for organizing but keyboard is better for writing.

2. Turn off all group notifications on all apps, on deskop and mobile. Leave unread badges on, and leave notifications on for DMs.

3. You cannot adopt inbox zero progressively. You must simply declare messaging bankruptcy and start from scratch. How? MARK AS READ for all messaging apps, ARCHIVE ALL for email. You won't miss anything I promise.

4. You do not use folders in any app. They will no longer be useful when you have no messaging debt.

5. You aren’t deleting. You are using unread/read as replacements for unfinished/finished. The only place where we remove messages is email (archive to preserve search).

Now, app by app strategies:

iMessage/Signal:

Always first priority, read & respond instantly. Priority not because high signal but because you can’t apply any inbox mgmt strategies.

Email:

1. Your inbox is a todo list

2. Read all emails as they come in (but don't reply)

3. Archive anything you don’t need to respond to
4. Use "skip it and archive" filtering for frequent messages (in Gmail, search bar for sender or subject, create a filter rule)

5. Unsubscribe from every newsletter as it comes in. If this isn’t working, you can create a filter. But you need to progressively eliminate spam as a high priority

6. When ready to reply on desktop, hit archive. Keep your inbox clean

Slack:

1. In order to clear: click groups with no mentions but don’t read, read & respond to groups with mentions

2.  Mute all groups with > 20, you can read on a Saturday if you want

3. Unread DMs, long hold and preview before reading. If easy, respond on phone. If not, leave and respond at desktop

Telegram/Whatsapp:

1. Two folders, Unread, and All

2. Mute all groups

3. In order: click in and out of groups with no mentions, then read and respond to groups with mentions

4. Handle DMs last, long hold and preview first. If instant, respond on phone. If not, leave and respond later.

5. Leave groups aggressively, don’t join any channels or social chats > 20 people. If you find yourself in one, leave.

X/LinkedIn/Instagram/etc.

1. Allow message requests from verified users

2. A lot of spam but can apply read/unread strategy

3. Read all to get started

I know this is lengthy but once you get the basics, you will build a new mental model of how to deal with messages from everywhere.

And you will soon have empty inboxes everywhere, allowing you to reply to new ones with tremendous speed.

Today, OFAC sanctioned an FBI Top 10 fugitive and Tren de Aragua member who allegedly stole millions from U.S. ATMs using malware loaded on Raspberry Pis — and laundered the proceeds through crypto.

Our investigators analyzed the on-chain network surrounding the now-sanctioned wallets. What we found: counterparties with exposure to known money laundering operations based in Mexico, Colombia, and Venezuela that have been used by drug cartels, smugglers, and other illicit actors.

While the underlying crimes differ, criminal organizations rely on common laundering infrastructure to move funds. ATM jackpotting proceeds flow through the same channels as drug trafficking money.
"The on-chain insights show us that criminal organizations are leveraging common infrastructure for laundering," said Chainalysis Senior Intelligence Analyst Kaitlin Martin. "These are insights that only the blockchain can provide."

We also found these networks heavily use stablecoins to move criminal proceeds globally. Stablecoins offer price stability, but they also leave these networks susceptible to advanced monitoring and instant freezing actions. 

This action is part of a broader government campaign: 30+ actions against 300+ individuals and entities tied to transnational criminal organizations since 2025. As these groups increasingly route funds through crypto, on-chain intelligence becomes critical.

quoted_text:
User interfaces are not going away. 

Yes, humans will use computers alongside agents. When working with agents, we will need the ability to audit what agents do in a human-readable way.

Yes, some interfaces (ex: dashboards, in-chat UI for ephemeral tasks, etc) will be generated. Most important interfaces will be intentionally designed. We will want both deterministic and non-deterministic interfaces in different situations. We're thinking a lot about the best ways to help designers shape non-deterministic systems at Figma.

Yes, new input modalities like voice, VR/AR and BCI will change the way we use computers and introduce lots of new interaction paradigms. This is all very exciting :)

Overall, the surface area of design will continue to grow much broader. Design is the new code and the key differentiator for software moving forward. Expect more and more energy to go into design / craft in the years ahead... it will be how you win or lose.

Eric is right about plenty of things, but the market will prove him wrong on this one...

🚨 WE HAVE A PERMITTING DEAL🚨  

And it is easily the best permitting bill we've ever gotten! 

- The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is HUGE (400+ pages) and both sides got a LOT. 

- The bill is much bigger and better than either Manchin post-IRA in 2022 or Manchin-Barrasso in 2024. 

Once I finish reading the text I'll publish an explainer. For now, here are a few high level takeaways. 

1. Transmission: The bill is absolutely HUGE for transmission, going further than Manchin-Barrasso. Includes: interregional transmission, limited federal backstop authority, interconnection queue reforms, directives for advanced grid-enhancing tech, and oversight of utilities. It's absolutely AMAZING all of this got in. 

2. NEPA: The bill has BIG changes to NEPA, including fixes for judicial review that underpins the law's costs. Still reading but this is even better than I expected! 

3. Certainty: The bill includes strong provisions to push back on misuse of permitting, like we're seeing with the admin's abuses against offshore wind. 

4. Historic Preservation: The bill includes changes to the NHPA 106 process, including changes to judicial review that will help right-size the process. 

5. Clean Water: The bill fixes problems with section 401 by adding new requirements for states and makes section 404 nationwide permits easier to comply with. 

6. Geothermal: The bill includes big wins for geothermal, including parity with oil and gas catexs. 

7. Mining: The bill fixes the "Rosemont decision" 

8. Endangered Species: The bill creates a new path for states to take on endangered species consultation. 

9. Hydro: Fixes for certain hydroelectric projects

10. Ratepayer protection: The bill adds protections for ratepayers from added data centers. Looks to be stronger than the House passed bill by quite a bit.

quoted_text:
I strongly believe trading is easiest when you're in a position of strength. One of the single greatest benefits of my entire trading career has been that I've always had a job & never used any trading income, I've always lived within the means of my job

There's never been a trade I "needed" to win to make rent or hit drinks with the boys or to buy the gf something nice. I could live off of my portfolio but choose not to because I don't think I could effectively manage the emotions of being reliant on my portfolio. If I somehow zero my port, at least my day to day life will not change

There are absolutely people who thrive on being all-in. I admire and respect tf out of you lunatics who chose to do so, I simply do not have that dog in me. I'm comfortable with my limits in that regard

The other benefit of having a job is that it keeps you in-touch with real people and the real world. Maybe since I now work for a crypto media company, I'm not the most in-touch guy on the planet. But I spend a lot of my day talking to young hungry clippers who haven't "made it" yet, I get to work with a bunch of creatives across many disciplines for awesome side projects we're working on, I have to make runs to FedEx to get stuff printed for the business, etc... Long story short, I interface with the real world, with real people, with real constraints that need to show up to work and answer to a higher power (their boss). That gives constant perspective I find immeasurably valuable

A quick little aside but I find tenured college professors and generally post-economic people who don't work some of the most insufferable people to spend time with. You remove so much of the human condition, but even worse you remove so much perspective on what people have to go through to get by. I find the detachment sustains outdated world views that are terrible for trading, but even worse - terrible for dinner conversation

Probably my number one trading advice is to actually get the best job you can, work hard, and grow your income. Become a cool person with skills outside of just trading, I promise they'll translate and you'll be trading from a position of strength

text:
A few thoughts after yesterday’s @OpenAI DevDay, from an engineering perspective.

The era of subsidized AI may be coming to an end.

OpenAI introducing a $500 plan, after the $200 tier already felt like unusually good value and was eventually constrained, is another signal that frontier intelligence probably won’t remain artificially cheap forever.

As these systems become more capable and more economically useful, we’ll likely start paying closer to their actual cost and value. I wouldn’t be surprised to see @AnthropicAI move in a similar direction.

But the more interesting shift to me is what’s happening to software itself.

OpenAI shipped what is essentially their equivalent of Jev in an incredibly short amount of time.
That should tell us something:
Software is losing its scarcity and big corp can take over your little idea anytime if it's attractive enough.

Products and features that would have required months of engineering, or looked technically unrealistic for a small team, can now be recreated remarkably quickly.

Building the feature is no longer the moat.
And paradoxically, I think this raises the bar for engineers rather than lowers it.

Craft, reliability, taste, performance, and obsessive attention to detail will matter more than ever. When almost anyone can generate functional software, differentiation moves toward how well the product is made and how deeply you understand the people using it.

Learn your audience. Talk to them. Build with them, not just for them.

Engineering > Product
I also don’t think AI kills engineering roles before it changes product roles.
Instead, I think a lot of traditional product thinking gets absorbed directly into engineering.
The strongest engineers will increasingly understand users, design, business, data, and distribution, and be able to execute across the entire loop:

understand the problem → build → ship → observe → talk to users → iterate.

The distinction between “product person” and “engineer” starts becoming much less meaningful when one person can do what previously required an entire team.

And if you’re a solo builder, there’s another skill you absolutely need to learn:

Distribution.

By now, anyone who has seriously built something understands this.
Building has never been cheaper.

When everyone can build, your edge becomes a combination of exceptional product quality, deep understanding of your users, and the ability to get that product in front of them. 
Hint: Think out of the box, way out, marketing has also changed and now Gen Z does it best.

text:
After 9 years. 16K+ family homes. 500M sqft inside real homes covered, we know home robots are being built in wrong order.

So we built Matic the way nature grows a child.

Finally, sharing our vision:
1.⁠ ⁠Why robots get stuck at the demo
2.⁠ ⁠Why labs can't ship robots
3.⁠ ⁠Why we started with eyes, not hands
4.⁠ ⁠The 99.999% rule in robotics
5.⁠ ⁠Where Matic is going next

1. Why most robots get stuck at demos

Robot demos look brilliant in a room arranged around its limitations: familiar lighting, predictable furniture, nothing troublesome on the floor.

A family’s home makes no such accommodations. There are cables, toys, shifting rugs and, occasionally, dog poop. Yes, humanoids will need to avoid that too.

Repeating a task under familiar conditions of uncluttered floors is not the same as handling an unfamiliar home with all its chaos.

2. Why labs can't ship robots

SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) is how a robot maps its surroundings and locates itself within them. Ask most academics and they'll tell you it's a solved problem.

But real homes are the most chaotic spaces that exist.

There are glass doors that look like open doorways, mirrors, stairs, rugs, charging cables, and Legos placed all around.

So ask yourself: if indoor mapping and navigation is "solved," where are the robots? Why aren't airports, hotels and grocery stores full of them?

Calling it “solved” misses the question families actually care about: can I leave this thing alone and trust it?

3. Why we started with eyes, not hands

Nature doesn't give birth to a fully working human. We took our cue from how nature develops humans: capabilities built on one another.
Children learn to see before they learn to grab, and to grab before they learn to plan and handle the unexpected.

Perception comes first. Manipulation follows. More complex responsibilities come after that. At every stage, the robot must earn the next job by doing its current one well enough.

Before asking a robot to pick up a sock, we wanted it to understand where it was, where the sock was, and how to reach it.

Most of the industry started at the top, with humanoids. We started at the bottom, with a robot whose job is to see and move through a home precisely with 1cm accuracy in any lighting condition.

Floor cleaning gave that foundation an immediately useful job. It forced us to confront navigation, clutter, privacy and everyday reliability before reaching for more complex chores.

The floor cleaner isn’t a detour from our larger ambition. It is how we’re building toward it.

4. The 99.999% rule in robotics

At 90%, one in ten decisions is wrong, and a robot makes thousands in a single clean. That's the robot that bumps, gets lost, and falls down the stairs.

Every extra nine is a new mountain. The failures get rarer, harder to find, and exponentially harder to fix. They barely even happen until they happen in your home.

Matic's visual SLAM runs at 99.999% in 16K+ homes. We’re the ONLY unsupervised home robot at scale with pure vision-only full autonomy.  If you ask us, the gap between 80% and 99.999% is where our 9 years of engineering went.

We close that gap inside real homes. When Matic handles something imperfectly, it saves a short clip and keeps it on the device. It only leaves if the family chooses to share it. If they do, it gets labeled, fed back into the model, and every Matic gets smarter, including theirs.

Families control what leaves their homes. We do the work of making the product better.

Better robots earn trust > trust brings more homes > and more homes teach the robot more.

5. Where Matic is going next

Phase one was perception and it's nearly done. Matic has covered 500 million square feet, 400K miles in thousands of real lived-in homes.
Now phase two is going to be about manipulation. And our idea is to build a robot that doesn't just move through your home, but acts in it to eliminate even more chores.

Each step must be useful today, not justified by something we promise tomorrow. The evolution of Matic is the revolution.

The goal isn’t to put the most impressive humanoid in your living room.

It’s giving your family time and energy back through robots that earn your trust, protect your privacy, and help without becoming another responsibility.

More time for each other. Less work getting in the way.

That’s Matic.
Get yours today at https://t.co/tEo81BKSmA

text:
我初次跑会应该是在 2017年 那个时代可以说机遇和骗子并存，后者可能更多一些，主要是那个阶段钱来的太容易了，所以只要你有钱，大家都会围着你。不过那个时候的很多人，即便是骗子也会把戏做足，我忘记了一个项目叫什么名字来着，融了 1,500 万 美元，所有的代码只有一行“Hello Word”。

那个时代的跑会，更多的还是在聊憧憬，聊加密货币是如何落地的，当时还没有叫 KOL 的说法，应该都是大V，尤其是火星，金色，巴比特有很多签约作者，写了不少好的文章。

转变应该是 2019年 发生的，2018年的时候 Fcoin 的交易即挖矿带火了交易所赛道，当时 ChainUp 等专门做交易所白标的是火的一塌糊涂，不论是小交易所还是盘子交易所，或者是一些有“志向”的小伙伴，都是从那时候开始的，这个时期就是 BD 非常的多了。

如果说以前跑会是情怀，那么2019年以后的跑会就开始商务起来了，当时的人均交易所 CEO 和现在的人均做市商或人均家办非常的相似，可惜是的随着 Fcoin 的倒闭，交易即挖矿还是回归历史了，交易所重新洗牌，大量的山寨交易所倒下了。

2020年的跑会就“悲情”了很多，但随着 2020年行情的转好，一个接一个天王项目的登场，当时的跑会还是有点看头的，起码你要懂跨链，懂支付，懂英文，才能聊起来几句，当时我已经开始跑香港了，香港的气氛确实好很多，国内的重点是放在波卡上。

2020年到2021年我个人觉得是加密货币最繁荣的时候，主流币涨，山寨币涨，Meme 币也在涨，当时已经开始逐渐出现 KOL 的身影，当然更多的还是在融资，喊单，社区和返佣上，当时的 KOL 很多背后都是绑定的项目方和交易所，那个时候也是钱最好赚的。

就是因为钱好赚，所以会发现谁都特别好交际，尤其是当时的聚会，买单的大哥一般都是矿工，交易所的小伙伴都是围着矿工，然后才是围着项目方。

到 2022年 和 2023年 市场一直就不好了，尤其是赶上了疫情阶段，国内的大会少了很多，但国外的大会非常的火，那两年我基本每个月都会飞一次，香港，日本，马来西亚，泰国，马耳他，美国，尤其是马耳他，16小时的行程，一年能飞三次，当时马耳他的交易所沙盒，很多交易所的小伙伴都头疼过。

2022年也是 NFT 火热的一年，2022年的市场聊 NFT 的非常多，而且很多发币的项目都在和 NFT 靠拢，当时还真不是很多人聊小图片，而是聊非同质化资产，最早的一批 STO 的项目就是从 NFT 演变出来的，那时候头像是只猴子就是社交圈里的大佬，猴子越多，“佬”越大。

很多交易社区也是从那个时候开始的，返佣社区化，区块链基础教育，带单老师也是从这个时期开始的，2022年交易员很多很多，当时的跑会很多都是听交易员讲量化，那时候量化一时风头无两，量化的概念我是 2020年开始接触的，2021年爆发，2022年开始重新洗盘。

2023年是第一次来新加坡，来的时候就非常喜欢，这个时期 X 当时还叫推特，已经开始是币圈的集散地了，出现了很多了不起的 KOL ，那个时候确实有那么一帮人就是在做无私的分享，2023年的香港和新加坡，论坛的质量非常的高，2023年已经很多人开始聊 Bitcoin 生态了，虽然已经是过去式，但那种全民讨论的情况好像在也没发生过了。

我还记得非常清楚，在 X 上，铭文和反铭文派天天吵架，但不是那种骂娘的吵架，很多人都在用代码说话，虽然挺闹腾的，但也挺有趣的。

2024年应该是 bitcoin:native 现货 ETF 的元年，从这一年开始，合规成了重点，2024年开始大会，重点都是在合规上了，也是从 2024年 开始，跑会的含金量开始下降了，虽然 Bitcoin 涨的不错，但山寨币的涨幅不行，很多重仓的小伙伴都跑的都没有干劲，那个时候更多的人还在研究市场和金融。

在 2024年对应的应该就是 Telegraph 生态了，Ton 的基金会在那个时候应该是最风光之一的了，然后就是 Ton 上的小程序，名字我都忘记了，但那个时候上币十个有七个是和 Ton 相关的，当时的跑会，你不认识几个 Ton 的人都没资格说自己是币圈的。

也是从 2024年 开始，我依稀记得跑会就开始乏味了，听不到什么建设性的东西，基本就是搞流量，不管你做什么都要和 Ton 绑定到一起才有流量，虽然都知道是假的，但这个泡沫当时就是大，Ton 的项目就是好上。

也是当时开始币圈分成了两派人，一派还是围绕 BTC 和主流币为主，讲合规，讲资本，讲华尔街，另一派就是围绕 Ton 和 Meme 生态为主，讲流量，讲社区，讲变现。

2025年开始的跑会重点是在 Alpha 上，上 Alpha 是当时的主角，一直到 2025年底，只要是跑会基本都是和 Alpha 有相关性，当时不论是正常的项目，还是盘圈的项目，都是想先上 Alpha ，以前需要上三线所得项目，当时只要上了 Alpha 就算是能交代了。

2024年到2025年也是 KOL 最活跃得一段时间，毕竟市场好，赚钱快，大巴项目方等着上币，上了币就空投，而且 2024年底随着 solana:6p6xgHyF7AeE6TZkSmFsko444wqoP15icUSqi2jfGiPN 得的出现，Meme 又火了起来，2025年除了 Alpha 应该就是 Meme 的发射和交易平台。

我如果没记错的话，2025年是 Meme 的KOL 最活跃的一年，几乎所有的会议，他们都是主角，即便是 Alpha 上 Meme 的项目都很多，当时也有两派，一派是传统派，走 Alpha + 合约的路线，一派是 Meme 发射的路线。

前者很多在 2025年底开始发财了，后者就看坐庄的人是谁了。对，从2025年下半年开始，有两个人从河内到了新加坡，开启了全民做市的浪潮。不是说这两个人带动了做市，而是说这两个人才让做市的市场这么热闹。

2026年就是做市商赚钱的一年，人均做市商就是从2026年春节以后开始的，4月开始在香港的时候基本碰到五个人就有三个说自己是做市商，还有一个是机构，一个是家办。一直到现在你问对方身份，和主要做的事情，很多人都会和你说一句，我和谁谁谁一起操盘的，XXX的项目就是我做的。

这一年最少有二十个不同的做市商团队说自己操作了同样“神盘”的项目，2026年，项目方尤其是有足够筹码的项目方是最受人欢迎的，只要知道你是项目方，酒池肉林就在向你招手了，谈项目，谈做市就是主线，项目方这两年应该是2021年以后最吃香的时候了。

这时候的 KOL 已经有很多人变成了白手套，毕竟在 2026年能赚钱的除了少数做交易的以外，赚钱并不那么容易，新项目越少，KOL 的竞争就越激烈，活下去就越难，不过 2025年和 2026年 越南确实逐渐成为了加密货币的发现之旅。

以前的越南都是韭菜，现在的越南随着逐渐合规，反而成为了支付，交易和返佣的洼地，越南 KOL 的含金量已经开始上升了，不论是短视频还是Youtube 甚至是Facebook 都有越南加密货币的身影。

所以我回顾了一下，对于跑会的这个话题，如果没有明确的目的，如果没有充足的预算，如果没有点斤两，跑会的含金量是在下降的，以前确实是有大哥愿意带新人，但现在大哥自己都很少出来了，除非是在一些私聚上，还能看到一些身影，大多小伙伴能接触的，基本都是来“跑会”的小伙伴。

社交挺好的，多认识一些人也没问题，攀攀交情也是正常的，甚至是见老朋友都是很正常的，但如果想要通过跑会能获得资源，期望能认识大哥，获得大哥的赏识，已经越来越难了。

中介二道贩子的生存空间已经越来越少了，认识人已经逐渐的从褒义词变成了贬义词，认识，可能只是停留在朋友圈，办事的还是要靠核心竞争力。

无他，感叹一下，这两年如果不是为了营业，我也不想跑了，但毕竟是要营业的，至于我的主营是什么，知道的小伙伴也就知道了，不知道的也就无需解释了。
author: PhyrexNi
quoted_text:
我记得那些在我什么都没有时帮过我的人，
很多时候跑会，不是为了认识更多人，
只是想着找个机会，再见见那些大哥、大姐们。
————————————
第一次跑会，是 2023 年初。
参加的是「村民活动中心年会」。

村民活动中心，
是华语区早期项目方 KOL 明哥发起的 DeFi 社区。
首批成员里，很多都来自江南愤青的社区。

江南愤青，
就是十年前金融圈里常被叫作「校长」的那位。

某种意义上，
2023年是我第一次真正走进Crypto & Web3的线下场。
——————————————————
为什么要特别提「华语早期」？
因为我第一次刷到明哥，是 2018 年。
那时候我还在想，要不要买 TRX。

江南愤青就更早了。
很多人的投资和投机底层，
其实都来自那个时代的 KOL。

和现在这批
「装头部」「借假修真」「装咖位」的 KOL 不一样的是，
2018 到 2023 年，我接触到的那批老师，是真的不装。
有判断，有成绩，也有脾气。

更重要的是：那时候的 KOL，是真的像个人。

最近很多人在 Diss 我，
或者讨论我和现在 KOL 圈的关系。
我想说的其实很简单：
你们现在看到的这批，算鸡毛。
我刚入圈时遇到的那些人，那才叫 KOL。
——————————————————
为什么会在 2023 年跑到杭州？

因为我在 2022 年毕业后，
进入撸毛圈的本金，来自「村里」。

没错！我最早期也是那种
亏完、迷茫、像个电子乞丐的人。

2022年毕业以后，
撸毛大半年没有见到什么结果。

钱快烧完了，所以到了 2023 年，
我已经走到了一个很现实的关口：
硕士毕业后的就业补助，马上就要错过最后期限了。

那时候想的也很简单：去杭州。
先想办法混上饭吃。

至于后来为什么没有去找工作？
因为去杭州没多久，
拜完「天下第一财神庙」没多久，
Arb 的空投来了。

那一波空投，
不只是让我第一次真正赚到钱。
更重要的是：
我第一次有了放弃就业的底气。

现在回头看，
2023 年的杭州，
可能就是我人生轨迹真正开始拐弯的地方。
——————————————————
同样的事情，
为什么去年我还会从马来西亚飞到上海，
参加 BlockFocus的酒会？

因为在我啥也不是、亏完的时候，
BlockFocus曾经一次又一次地捞我一把。

为什么过去两年，我都会飞日本去见枪总？
因为我入圈后最早的两次不错的 KOL Round，
以及 M，都来自……

这些在我什么都没有的时候，
愿意给我机会的人，
我一直都记得，
然后这两年好转后，
我还是不要脸的蹭吃蹭喝的状态。

我其实不是一个喜欢主动社交的人，
但我还是很愿意，
定期去见一见这些大哥、大姐。
因为我始终觉得：
人可以忘记自己赚过多少钱，
但不应该忘记谁在自己什么都没有的时候，
愿意给过机会。

所以我去跑这些会，
有时候不是为了认识更多人。
而是想去见见那些
在我还啥也不是的时候，

A data center can lower your electricity bill. a16z's Alex Immerman, David George, and Sarah Wang on the myth that gets the least pushback and deserves the most:

"It may seem counterintuitive, but a data center can help lower your electricity rate. A recent US study showed that for every 10% increase in data center capacity, residential rates went down by 40 bps."

"You should think about it as a power grid is a shared fixed cost base: poles, wires, substations. A large stable customer, like a data center, can help spread those costs across more units of electricity. Simply put, more demand across a shared system is a positive."

"Investment in shared infrastructure can also improve the economics for the households and businesses connected to it."

"I don't think that point gets enough media attention. Dina Powell went on a podcast recently from Meta and talked about the Louisiana site that they did, where they worked with the community to lower electricity costs. There's real examples of that today. It's not just lip service."

quoted_text:
a16z's David George, Sarah Wang, Alex Immerman, and Santiago Rodriguez on the State of Markets, from AI and infrastructure to the next investment cycles:

1. Tech is the everything cycle.

High-tech equipment, software, and R&D are now about 55% of US capital spending, and the AI buildout just passed the railroads as a share of GDP. The five largest hyperscalers will spend about $780B on capex this year, heading past $1T in 2027, and demand still outstrips supply at every point in the chain.

2. It's an earnings story.

Stocks are up about 20% while multiples are down about 20%, and the S&P trades under 20x earnings. The market is up 90% since ChatGPT, on 15% earnings growth.

3. AI adoption is broad and shallow.

69% of the S&P 500 has a live AI deployment, 30% report a quantified result, and just 2% have AI doing a job they'd notice if it stopped. The power users are pulling away: the top 1% of AI spenders spend eight times the top 10%.

4. The private markets are enormous.

Six private companies, Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, and Revolut, add up to about $2.4T by last round, more than every IPO of the past decade combined. "The founder is the asset class. The IPO is another financing event."

Plus: why a data center can lower your electricity bill, what Amazon saying no to Muse and Instacart saying yes tells you about marketplaces, and the seven areas the team is most excited about next.

text:
$GOOGL UNVEILS GEMINI 4 ARGON

Google unveiled Gemini 4 Argon, its new frontier model and the top model in the Gemini 4 generation.

Here’s everything you need to know:

Pricing: $2 per 1M input tokens and $10 per 1M output tokens, with cached input priced 95% lower.

Output limit: Argon can generate up to 1 million output tokens in a single trajectory, up from 64K previously.

Performance: Google says Argon is competitive with OpenAI’s Astra and Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 across coding, enterprise work and cybersecurity. It leads several published benchmarks, including:

Vals Index: 68.9%  
AutomationBench: 51.3%  
Finance Agent v2: 65.4%  
DeepSWE v1.1: 77.9%  
LVBench: 91.7%

Internal use at Google: Argon is already being used by thousands of employees.

Google says Argon agents identified memory optimizations that freed more than 300 TiB across its data centers, with an estimated 500 TiB to 1 PiB of total savings.

It also helped optimize a quantum computing subroutine by 40%, and is being used for large-scale C/C++ to Rust migrations, including 800K+ lines for the Fuchsia Zircon kernel.

Cybersecurity: Argon scored 68% on CWE-bench v1, tying for the top score, and Google says it can autonomously find, validate and patch software vulnerabilities.

Trusted cybersecurity partners will get access without the model’s normal cyber guardrails so they can use its full defensive capabilities.

Availability: Argon is initially rolling out to select cyber defenders and Google’s internal teams.

Google says broader access will come later, starting with paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers, but no public release date was given.

Google is also participating in the Trump administration’s voluntary pre-release model access process before wider availability

text:
My first OBSERVATIONS from Sundar's Gemini 4 Argon announcement:

1. Quantum. Google's quantum researchers gave Argon a key piece of quantum software to shrink, and in minutes it found a version that needs 40% fewer qubits and operations than the best published human solution. 

Quantum computers are useful ONLY once programs fit on the hardware, so this pulls that date closer from the software side, and it also shortens the time banks and governments have to switch to encryption quantum can't break.

2. Data center memory. A team of Argon agents read Google's server data, found waste, and freed over 300 TiB of memory on their own, with up to 1 PiB expected. 

If agents can do this everywhere, companies will point them at their cloud bills before buying more servers, and some of the huge data center buildout may turn out to need less hardware than planned.

3. Rewriting old code. Argon agents are converting Google's old C and C++ code into Rust, a safer language, including an 800K- ine operating system kernel.

There are PLENTY of companies stay with outdated software vendors only because switching is painful, and once rewriting is cheap, that lock in starts to break!

4. Faster than the engineers. On one video decoder, Argon ran 100s of experiments and ended up 2.7x faster than the version Google's own engineers wrote. Speeding up your slowest code used to take a specialist team, and now it's something you can run overnight and pay for based on the savings.

5. Million-token answers. The most a model could write in one answer went from 64K tokens to 1 million, enough for a whole codebase or a full due diligence report.

Obviously, nobody can carefully review that much output, so the bottleneck moves from making things to checking them, and tools that verify AI work become a big market.

6. Two versions of the same model. Vetted security teams get Argon with the cyber safety limits removed, and everyone else gets the restricted one. 

The best defense goes to big trusted organizations first, which leaves smaller companies more exposed and creates demand for services that get them "trusted" status. Gotta think about this more and what it means.

7. Finding bugs faster than anyone can fix them. Wiz used Argon to find a serious security hole in hospital software used worldwide that every earlier model missed. When AI can find holes this fast, the pile of known but unpatched bugs becomes the real risk, and whoever makes patching fast wins.

8. Legal work. On Harvey's legal benchmark Argon scored 19.6%, and every other top model was under 7%, the biggest gap in the whole chart!! 

Harvey, a startup, built that test, and now Google launches on it, so owning the benchmark in your industry gives you leverage over the labs.

9. Promo pricing. It launches at $2 in and $10 out per million tokens, about a 20% ish  of GPT6's price, and then doubles. Startups that set their prices on the promo rate will see margins shrink in a few months, even though everyone assumes AI only gets cheaper.

10. Cheap memory. Reused context is 95% off. Products that keep one big shared knowledge base and reuse it across users will run far cheaper than rivals that resend everything each time.

11. Watching the model. Google seals Argon's test environment before training, watches its reasoning live, can stop it mid task, and asked other labs to keep reasoning readable. 

Companies running their own agents will copy this, and monitoring and permissions for AI agents turns into its own product category.

12. Government first. The US government gets access before the public through a voluntary review. 

DC is pretty much the first customer now, and launch dates start depending on its review, not only on when the model is ready. That's the new normal, I guess since the Fable/Mythos debacle.

I'll share more on Gemini 4 as it comes out on @startupideaspod 

Never a dull moment in AI, isn't it?

text:
谷歌发布新一代旗舰模型 Gemini 4 Argon。

谷歌在跑分表里拿它和 OpenAI 的 GPT-6 Astra、Anthropic 的 Claude Fable 5.1 和 Claude Opus 5.5 对比，价格却定在 GPT-6.1 Sol 和 Opus 5.5 的档位。

普通用户和开发者暂时还用不上，第一批只开放给谷歌 Fairwind 计划里的网络安全防御人员。

谷歌说会分阶段放开，同时参与美国政府的模型发布前自愿审查流程，也就是正式发布前先让政府访问模型。之后先开放给付费 API 客户和 Google AI Ultra 订阅用户，再到普通消费者，具体日期没有公布。

首发优惠价是每百万输入 token 2 美元、每百万输出 token 10 美元，和 GPT-6.1 Sol 完全相同。优惠期结束后是 4 美元和 20 美元，和 Claude Opus 5.5 相同。

GPT-6 Astra 和 Claude Fable 5.1 都是 10 美元和 50 美元，也就是说即使恢复原价，Argon 也只要它们的五分之一。命中缓存的输入按原价的 5% 收费，同样与 Sol 和 Opus 5.5 持平。token 是模型计算文字量的单位，一百万 token 大约相当于 75 万个英文单词。

规格上最大的变化是输出上限：单次最多输出 100 万 token，上一代是 6.4 万。

GPT-6 Astra、GPT-6.1 Sol、Claude Fable 5.1 和 Opus 5.5 目前都是 12.8 万，Argon 是它们的将近 8 倍。

按谷歌的说法，模型可以在一次任务里连续思考、生成几十万 token，难题不用拆成很多轮来做。

谷歌说已有数千名员工在日常工作中使用它，并举了几个内部例子：

量子计算团队用它优化量子算法的资源消耗（量子比特数乘以门操作数），其中一例几分钟内就比已发表的基准方案好 40%。

一组 Argon 智能体分析谷歌数据中心的内存使用数据，自动找出并应用优化，已释放超过 300 TiB 内存，谷歌估计总共能省下 500 TiB 到 1 PiB。

Argon 智能体正在把谷歌的 C/C++ 代码迁移到 Rust。Rust 是一种从语言层面避免大部分内存安全漏洞的编程语言。迁移规模从几万行的基础库，到 80 多万行的 Fuchsia 系统 Zircon 内核，上线前都要经过自动和人工审核、测试。在视频解码库 libgav1 的 Rust 版本里，智能体把 3.2 万行手写的底层加速代码换成了编译器能自动优化的安全 Rust 代码，速度是原 Rust 版的 2.7 倍，解码出的画面完全一致。

谷歌的对比表一共 19 项测试，Argon 13 项第一，1 项和 Astra 并列第一，5 项落后。以下分数均为谷歌公布，顺序是 Argon、Astra、Fable 5.1、Opus 5.5。

领先最明显的是专业工作。Harvey 的法律智能体测试考法律检索和文书起草，Argon 19.6%，其他三家是 5.4%、6.7%、3.8%。金融研究测试 Vals Finance Agent v2 是 65.4%，对手是 53.5%、58.9%、58.6%。Zapier 的 AutomationBench 考从头到尾完成企业业务流程，Argon 51.3%，对手是 41.4%、31.4%、42.5%。按美国 GDP 加权、覆盖金融编程法律税务的综合榜 Vals Index 上差距小一些，68.9% 对 63.1%、65.8%、67.0%。

超长材料也是强项。GraphWalks 测模型在长文本里追踪信息之间的关系，材料长度在 25.6 万到 100 万 token 时，Argon 84.2%，其他三家是 71.8%、65.0%、66.8%。长视频理解 LVBench 上 Argon 91.7%，对手是 87.5%、79.7%、83.7%。

编程有输有赢。考长流程真实软件工程任务的 DeepSWE v1.1 上 Argon 77.9%，对手是 74.1%、67.4%、74.2%。但在另一项软件工程测试 FrontierSWE v2 上 Argon 只有 55.0%，四家里最低，Astra 65.5% 第一。在考命令行操作的 Terminal-bench 4.0 上 Argon 57.4%，也是四家最低，Opus 5.5 以 66.4% 领先。

另外三项落后的：机器学习工程 PostTrainBench，Opus 5.5 第一（49.3% 对 Argon 45.3%）；科学计算 Terminal-Bench Science，Astra 第一（68.1% 对 57.6%）；操作电脑的 OSWorld-2.0，Astra 第一（72.6% 对 69.2%），这一项表里没有 Claude 的分数。

网络安全是这次发布的重点。谷歌专门训练 Argon 做安全防御：自动找漏洞、验证漏洞、打补丁。给受信任防御人员和谷歌内部团队的版本不带网络安全方面的限制，可以用上全部能力。

安全公司 Wiz 已在它的免费公益项目 Scan for Good 里使用 Argon。据谷歌介绍，Argon 在全球医院使用的一款医疗软件里发现了一个严重漏洞，可能泄露敏感个人信息，之前的前沿模型都没发现。在测试漏洞修复能力的 CWE-bench v1 上，Argon 和 GPT-6 Astra 都是 68%，并列第一，Opus 5.5 是 67%，Fable 5.1 是 58%。谷歌称，它发现漏洞的能力比上一代安全专用模型 3.8 Flash Cyber 明显更强。

在大范围开放前，谷歌列了四项安全措施：

拒绝协助网络攻击和化学、生物、放射性、核武器方面的有害请求，并通过监测模型内部的激活状态来识别滥用。

防提示词注入，也就是有人在网页或文件里藏恶意指令来劫持模型。谷歌称 Argon 在 Gray Swan 的间接提示词注入测试中领先。

监控模型的思考过程和实际操作，发现它做出超出用户意图的事就中止执行。训练阶段也有类似监控，谷歌称没有把监控结果用回训练，以免模型学会躲避监控。

在高风险训练和测试开始前，把运行模型的沙箱环境隔离封闭。

text:
I asked Secretary Duffy what Americans should be able to do, if we get this decade right, that they can't do today.

Sean Duffy is the Secretary of Transportation, and he sat down with me at our Startup Industrial Base event in DC today. He went straight to how our country's air traffic gets managed.

At the command center, people sit in front of six screens with a paper flight chart above them, trying to make the calls on weather and routing.

His example: four planes reach the same runway at the same time and only one can land. See it two hours out, speed up two, slow one down, and each one lands when the runway is open. "Like, not complicated stuff, but we don't do any of this."

Paper and pencil and minimal human augmentation from software looks like this: Say an airport can take 15 planes in a 15 minute window. "Well, the airlines will schedule 32." He says he's handing the airlines that data and asking them to spread out.

The tool is SMART, from Air Space Intelligence, a small company he says competed with the biggest companies and won. It predicts. His stage example: a 2.5 hour ground stop might only need 45 minutes. He's taken heat for supposedly handing air traffic control to AI. Duffy's answer? "it's dumb AI, not smart AI." Controllers still make every call.

None of this needs a breakthrough. It needs the will of the people to know they need to use software and be ok with AI augmentation instead of insisting on a paper chart and copper wire.

Google has a pretty unfair loop with Argon compared to the rest of frontier labs

they own the TPUs underneath Argon and can drop the model straight into APIs already processing around 22B tokens/min. 

Thats a pretty impressive setup. 

Build the chips -> train the model -> ship it into absurd distribution -> feed the gains back to the next run. 

And Argon is already improving the stack around itself too, freeing up 300+ TiB of datacenter memory by migrating +800k lines from C/C++ to Rust and pushing a quantum-computing routine 40% past the published baseline. 

Every Gemini generation can increasingly inherit infrastructure the previous one helped optimize

Argon is likely the best/only version of full-stack advantage we've seen in western frontier labs.

text: An era of agentic mathematics is on. And boy, it's so fun to see shapes of theories and curate new proofs from very rough ideas. Soon annoucements of nice results in algebraic geometry and non-commutative algebra. What's the strangest part is that I really do collaborate with the machine and see the models generalize from symbolic computations, propose new conjectures, explore proof space by deforming arguments and so on. And you don't need to digest everything, just critical ideas. Once you do, you can give key directions to your harness and steer the discovery. Lean finishes the proofs but in the end of the day you already digested everything critical. Lean is just a documentation that nothing got wrong, the proof blueprint is already in your head because of the interaction with the agentic harness.
author: nasqret
quoted_text:
Thanks! Yes, I use a combination of Codex CLI (with Astra Max) and Claude Code (with Opus 5.5 Max). I start my projects with Astra for the heavy grinding, the most tricky part is the setup with knowledge base, initial division of work, management of the agents which either process existing knowledge or they guess new stuff (by deforming existing arguments). It's like having many crawlers that penetrate the field by exploring in very small steps. I rely heavily on numerical computations which help the agents to get more confidence in the claims they make (or even make new claims based on the numerics). My harness is basically a very carefully setup agentic workflow in standard Codex and CC. Of course the big jump happens when I target the models on a specific task (but not too specific). In the work on Laman graphs I actually forced Astra to proof a central genus characterization result. Then, I switched to Opus for write-up and started building a new knowledge base (in parallel) with more digested versions of proofs. So now Astra is formalizing discoveries and Opus is exploring the related results and seeing what new conjectures we can already cover with the existing knowledge base. 

I still do a lot of human interventions, i.e. I give text commands after each work campaign to focus the workflow on specific targets (like bootstrapping genera bounds etc.) This is quite remarkable that if you have an intuition which tools are needed you can push those agents to finish a lot of results for you for free.

I think what is also important in this approach is that you accept that models will prove things which are not really original statements from your questions. You let them freely explore the proof space. After several dry runs the agents stabilize, because the knowledge base gets pretty large and they split into groups doing ideation, proof generation, coding experiments, revising proofs or formalizing them. It's like a little proof factory where every agent has a very specific role to play. 

And I don't need 10k agents to do stuff, but I tend to be super focused and rely more on human intuition and slow digestion of some key directions. I am really trying to understand "the shape of what's possible", not just stupidly process large number of meaningless statements. 

In this approach you can also see that some fields of mathematics are slightly more amenable. If you can make a heavy numerical experiment (symbolically with Python or Rust), then you get access to very effective intuition compiler. text:
Jeff might be the worst businessman in crypto.

He didn’t raise the money.

He didn’t chase exchange listings.

He didn’t build a huge team.

He even reportedly turned down a ~$100M investment offer when Hyperliquid was valued around $1B.

From the outside, it looked almost stubborn.

Then the numbers started making the argument for him.

Hyperliquid processed roughly $2.95T in trading volume and generated about $844M in revenue in 2025, according to ecosystem reporting.

The team was reported to be just 11 people.

No VC-controlled cap table.
No traditional exchange empire behind it.

Just an obsession with building the product.

And the part I find most interesting is where that obsession came from.

Jeff grew up with a single mother who worked overtime. In eighth grade, he discovered competitive mathematics and realised other kids had been preparing for years.

So he started waking up at 5am and solving old competition papers by himself.

That same mentality eventually took him through physics olympiads, high-frequency trading, Chameleon, and finally Hyperliquid.

Maybe Hyperliquid didn’t become what it is because Jeff knew how to build a crypto company.

Maybe he simply knew how to obsess over a problem until everyone else had to take the result seriously.
author: Dmyonhl
quoted_text:
Some days on the Hyperliquid calendar should never be treated like normal days.

Because behind all these numbers is a pretty unusual story.

Jeff Yan grew up in Redwood Shores, in a family that wasn’t particularly wealthy compared with the people around him.

His parents divorced when he was in third grade. His mother worked overtime as an accountant.

Nobody pushed him toward some grand career.

Then, in eighth grade, a friend took him to a math competition. I think he got obsessed.

The following summer, he woke up at 5am, downloaded old competition papers, and solved them alone in his room. No tutor. No summer program.
Nobody telling him to do it.

Just something he genuinely wanted to get better at.

A few years later, he was on the US Physics Olympiad team.

Then came a gold medal at the International Physics Olympiad, ranking 24th in the world.

Fast forward to today.

That same obsession produced Hyperliquid. With 11 people.

$900M+ in 2025 profit, according to the Colossus profile.

$4T+ in cumulative trading volume.

And a company that was valued at roughly $10B in value without taking VC funding. 

But this is the part I find more interesting.

Hyperliquid now has its own calendar of moments worth remembering.

Nov 29, 2024. 310M HYPE. 31% of the total supply. Distributed to more than 90,000 early users. No private investor allocation. 

Feb 18, 2025. HyperEVM went live.

Apr 21, 2025. The validator set became fully permissionless.

Oct 13, 2025. HIP-3 went live.

And now we’re watching HYPE become something much bigger than the token that launched that November morning.

These are the days I want to remember.
The days when something changed.

author: ScottWu46
quoted_text:
We are terminating Chris Degnan for unethical conduct involving Cognition.

The last few months have seen incredible progress in AI capabilities. San Francisco has flourished as new companies that solve new, more ambitious problems are finding great success. Generally, it is a wonderful time to be building.

We at @FactoryAI have seen overwhelming interest in our model-agnostic coding agents and our software factory product. Our team has 10x’d in size, while our revenue has 100x’d year over year. This momentum has been unprecedented.

A much larger competitor, Cognition (makers of Devin) has fallen behind us on the capabilities that matter most to customers: cost, quality, and security. Instead of competing in the market, Cognition engineers feigned interviews with us to pry information about our product. Not finding what they were looking for, Cognition has decided to throw their weight and money at people with direct knowledge of our most confidential plans.

It feels as though ethics is being thrown out of the window in the AI era. People are willing to do anything, including exploiting privileged information and violating ethical boundaries. I think this is unique to our time, and I don’t think it’s right. Integrity still matters.

Yesterday, I made the decision to immediately terminate Christopher Degnan’s roles as a Board Observer and Advisor to Factory, after over a year of service.

Prior to this decision, Chris told me he had a casual conversation with an executive at Cognition AI. When I questioned his intentions, he reassured me that ethics aside, he had “made too much money” and was “too lazy to go work for Cognition,” which I trusted and believed.

On Monday, Chris spent time advising the Factory team on a handful of confidential board-level matters. That evening, he called me to say that the conversation that was initially described as casual and one-off was actually formal and recurring. For weeks, while he sat in our board meetings and advised our leadership team, he was also confiding with executives of our largest competitor. Chris was subject to confidentiality obligations in connection with his work with Factory. We do not know the extent of the information he shared, but it puts his timely questions about our product roadmap and what the parity gap involves into a new light.

It is sad to sever a relationship with someone who has been a trusted advisor - and even a close friend -  for over a year. But Chris’s conduct is unacceptable to me. Trust in Board Membership is one of the sacred bonds in the Silicon Valley, one that helps the startup ecosystem thrive. With it comes an enormous responsibility. That trust was violated.

Competition is good. I respect and in many cases admire our competitors. San Francisco is a beautiful, singular place where the bold and ambitious go to defy the norms and precedents of the past. But certain principles that must remain. Violating ethics to seek advantage turns what should be positive-sum into zero-sum.

We all love technology. And we all love to compete. But we must hold ourselves to a higher standard. The future of software engineering comes with abundance that will impact every person on Earth. Building that future comes with immense responsibility. We must build and compete with integrity.

author: lex_node
quoted_text:
@RAILGUN_Project and @0xprivacypools get flak for sanctions checks, but neither can freeze or take your funds without notice.

RAILGUN: screening is client side, and a flagged shield can still unshield back to its origin. Confiscating funds would take a smart contract upgrade,  which requires a RAIL vote--a form of public due process--with the exact calldata onchain 7+ days before execution. and no confiscation policy is currently contemplated. 

Privacy Pools: the ASP can withhold approval, which forces a public ragequit to your deposit address. Deanonymization, not seizure.

to me this is the line of "permissionless but not lawless "...anyone can use these systems with no fear of funds seizure, but there are legal protections that may nerf certain features...

text:
마이크론 SCA, 직전 분기 대비 달라진 점

체결 16건 → 26건, 고객 재무 약정 $220억 → $320억

1. 계약 건수 증가

직전 분기(3Q FY26) 16건에서 이번 분기 26건으로 늘었음. 체결된 계약만으로 2030년까지 매출의 35% 이상을 확보할 것으로 추정.

직전 분기에 제시한 "전체 완료 시 매출의 약 절반"은 앞으로 체결할 계약까지 포함한 목표치임. 35%는 이미 체결된 계약만 기준이라 두 숫자를 바로 비교하긴 어렵고, 목표치에 근접해짐.

2. 계약 기간 2031년으로 연장

기존 계약은 2030년까지였는데, 이번에 2031년까지 가는 계약을 새로 체결했고 기존 2건도 1년 연장함. 회사 설명으로는 고객들이 2030년 이후 물량까지 확보하길 원하고 있음.

고객 입장에서 공급 확보가 여전히 급하다는 신호

3. 가격 구조 구체화, 신규 계약은 더 비싸게

SCA 추정 매출의 4분의 3은 가격 체계가 있고 대부분이 최저가·최고가 밴드 방식임. 나머지 4분의 1은 시장가 기준으로 주기적으로 재협상함. 새로 논의 중인 계약은 현재 시황을 반영해 더 높은 가격에 협상 중이라고 함.

초기 계약보다 조건이 마이크론에 유리해지고 있다는 뜻으로 읽힘.

4. 고객 재무 약정 $320억

직전 분기에 예상한 $220억에서 $320억으로 늘었고, 대부분이 현금 예치금임.

고객이 선불로 capex 일부를 부담해주는 구조가 더 커지는 것이라, 메모리 사이클 변동성을 줄이는 효과는 커지는 듯.

*삼성,하이닉스도 이런 장기계약 맺었을텐데 마이크론처럼 구체적으로 얘기해줬으면 좋겠음.

For years, maybe a decade, I've wanted to build a writing tool that just did a few things I couldn't find anywhere else.

A system that mimicked how I think when I write. A system that provided clear affordances, features, and places to do the things I wanted to do. A way to play with my writing as I'm writing it. A way to settle into just the right way to say something.

It never made sense to make it a 37signals product because it's not commercially viable, nor would it be worth pulling people off their other work to hack on this. Plus, it would have taken months the old way.

So this weekend I just made it myself, with Claude's help.

It's called Write_On and the short video walks you through it.

Essentially it's "alternative control" at the word, sentence, and paragraph level, plus a way to dim stuff back, and stash stuff near by. Not version control, but alternative control. You'll see what I mean when you watch the video below.

So here it is. Write_On.

What's an agent bootcamp? 
A 5-day, free intensive to find & build high-impact agent opportunities with your real systems & data.

text:
My first OBSERVATIONS from Sundar's Gemini 4 Argon announcement:

1. Quantum. Google's quantum researchers gave Argon a key piece of quantum software to shrink, and in minutes it found a version that needs 40% fewer qubits and operations than the best published human solution. 

Quantum computers are useful ONLY once programs fit on the hardware, so this pulls that date closer from the software side, and it also shortens the time banks and governments have to switch to encryption quantum can't break.

2. Data center memory. A team of Argon agents read Google's server data, found waste, and freed over 300 TiB of memory on their own, with up to 1 PiB expected. 

If agents can do this everywhere, companies will point them at their cloud bills before buying more servers, and some of the huge data center buildout may turn out to need less hardware than planned.

3. Rewriting old code. Argon agents are converting Google's old C and C++ code into Rust, a safer language, including an 800K- ine operating system kernel.

There are PLENTY of companies stay with outdated software vendors only because switching is painful, and once rewriting is cheap, that lock in starts to break!

4. Faster than the engineers. On one video decoder, Argon ran 100s of experiments and ended up 2.7x faster than the version Google's own engineers wrote. Speeding up your slowest code used to take a specialist team, and now it's something you can run overnight and pay for based on the savings.

5. Million-token answers. The most a model could write in one answer went from 64K tokens to 1 million, enough for a whole codebase or a full due diligence report.

Obviously, nobody can carefully review that much output, so the bottleneck moves from making things to checking them, and tools that verify AI work become a big market.

6. Two versions of the same model. Vetted security teams get Argon with the cyber safety limits removed, and everyone else gets the restricted one. 

The best defense goes to big trusted organizations first, which leaves smaller companies more exposed and creates demand for services that get them "trusted" status. Gotta think about this more and what it means.

7. Finding bugs faster than anyone can fix them. Wiz used Argon to find a serious security hole in hospital software used worldwide that every earlier model missed. When AI can find holes this fast, the pile of known but unpatched bugs becomes the real risk, and whoever makes patching fast wins.

8. Legal work. On Harvey's legal benchmark Argon scored 19.6%, and every other top model was under 7%, the biggest gap in the whole chart!! 

Harvey, a startup, built that test, and now Google launches on it, so owning the benchmark in your industry gives you leverage over the labs.

9. Promo pricing. It launches at $2 in and $10 out per million tokens, about a 20% ish  of GPT6's price, and then doubles. Startups that set their prices on the promo rate will see margins shrink in a few months, even though everyone assumes AI only gets cheaper.

10. Cheap memory. Reused context is 95% off. Products that keep one big shared knowledge base and reuse it across users will run far cheaper than rivals that resend everything each time.

11. Watching the model. Google seals Argon's test environment before training, watches its reasoning live, can stop it mid task, and asked other labs to keep reasoning readable. 

Companies running their own agents will copy this, and monitoring and permissions for AI agents turns into its own product category.

12. Government first. The US government gets access before the public through a voluntary review. 

DC is pretty much the first customer now, and launch dates start depending on its review, not only on when the model is ready. That's the new normal, I guess since the Fable/Mythos debacle.

I'll share more on Gemini 4 as it comes out on @startupideaspod 

Never a dull moment in AI, isn't it?

text:
Nvidia has now a big problem.

China built an AI that writes CUDA better than humans experts.

Writing high-performance CUDA kernels for GPUs has always been a black art. It requires a brutal, microscopic understanding of hardware architecture, memory hierarchies, and parallel processing.

Even the best LLMs have traditionally choked on it, completely outperformed by old-school compilers like torch.compile.

ByteDance and Tsinghua University dropped a paper introducing “CUDA Agent.”

It is a large-scale agentic reinforcement learning system that transforms LLMs from passive code-completers into active, autonomous hardware optimizers.

Instead of guessing code in one shot, the agent runs in a continuous, multi-turn loop. It writes code, compiles it, profiles the hardware bottlenecks, catches its own bugs, and rewrites it.

The results completely shatter previous benchmarks.

It didn't just match static compilers. It left them in the dust.

• 2.11× faster than torch.compile • 2.60× faster than standard eager mode

• Achieved a massive 98.8% pass rate on complex kernel generation tasks

It discovered advanced operator-fusion techniques that static compiler heuristics can't even see.

For years, we’ve assumed that while AI can write web apps and python scripts, deep hardware-level optimization would require human engineering for a long time.

That assumption just expired.

The models aren't just writing software anymore.

They are optimizing the silicon it runs on.

text:
What if the dividend checks from your dullest holdings are the reason you can hold your most volatile winners?

✍️

I think of a portfolio like a garden with two kinds of plants: the ones that feed you every season and the ones that take years before they bear fruit. Most people argue about which is better. I’d rather let them support each other.

Steady cash flow doesn’t just add dollars—it changes behavior. When part of the portfolio pays you while you wait, you’re less likely to panic when the growth names get loud and unpredictable. A reliable dividend is a seatbelt. It keeps you in the car when the road gets bumpy.

That’s how my Portfolio is built. The rent comes in from a landlord like Realty Income. It’s not exciting, and that’s the point. Those checks give me room to keep owning a company like NVIDIA without needing to guess the next headline or quarter. The cash flow funds the patience. It also sets a rhythm: every month, new money shows up, and the question becomes simple—where does it do the most good for the next decade?

This mix also protects the plan. If growth stalls for a time, the cash still shows up. If the dividend side goes quiet, the growth side can carry compounding through innovation. It’s not about chasing yield or worshiping growth. It’s about building a portfolio I can actually stick with when the market tests my nerves.

Over decades, staying invested matters more than being clever. For me, dependable cash flow is the tool that makes staying invested easier.

Which role do you prioritize in your own portfolio—the payer that funds patience, or the grower that tests it—and how do you link the two so they make each other stronger?

text:
Why Tokenization Could Be the Most Important Economic Innovation of Our Lifetime | Bruce Fenton

@BruceFenton  is a longtime Bitcoin advocate since 2012, securities professional, and one of the early pioneers of tokenized securities. He is the founder and CEO of Chainstone Labs and founder of Atlantic Financial.

Alongside Overstock founder @PatrickByrne, Bruce was involved in some of the earliest efforts to bring securities and financial-market infrastructure onto blockchain rails. In 2018, he tokenized equity in his own company, Chainstone Labs, on the Ravencoin blockchain—years before tokenization became one of Wall Street’s biggest narratives.

In this episode, Bruce breaks down naked short selling, the plumbing behind traditional securities markets, and why he believes much of the problem is ultimately a ledger problem. We dive into questions such as: Who actually owns the stocks sitting in your brokerage account? How can shares be lent and rehypothecated? What role do brokers, clearing firms, DTCC, and Cede & Co. play in determining who owns what? And could blockchain replace an opaque system of claims and intermediaries with a transparent ledger showing exactly where an asset is and who owns it?

We unpack what “tokenized stocks” actually means—and the important distinction between a token that simply gives you exposure to a stock’s price and a security issued natively onchain, where the token itself represents the actual share and the ownership rights that come with it.

Bruce discusses how tokenization could allow smaller businesses to tokenize ownership and have their stock traded globally without needing to be listed on a traditional exchange like the NYSE, as well as what a future without KYC could look like. Finally, we get into Wall Street’s embrace of tokenization, the SEC’s evolving approach to tokenized securities, and one of the biggest questions surrounding the future of this technology: who ultimately controls these new financial rails?

The #1 life hack to becoming more productive, to becoming respected & trusted by everyone you work with:

Responding to every message within seconds or minutes and rarely hours.

It is no secret that the world's busiest and most successful people are also the fastest to respond.

But how does one become hyper responsive?

You adopt a rigorous strategy across all of your messaging surfaces. The goal is to eliminate overall noise, and never have a large pileup of messages such that the mental overhang of responding becomes a problem.

Here is my comprehensive personal messaging strategy that I’ve employed in some fashion for over 20 years to be the most responsive person you know.

First, some global rules:

1. You will process but not respond to most messages by phone. You will respond to most on your laptop. Why? Touch interface is fast for organizing but keyboard is better for writing.

2. Turn off all group notifications on all apps, on deskop and mobile. Leave unread badges on, and leave notifications on for DMs.

3. You cannot adopt inbox zero progressively. You must simply declare messaging bankruptcy and start from scratch. How? MARK AS READ for all messaging apps, ARCHIVE ALL for email. You won't miss anything I promise.

4. You do not use folders in any app. They will no longer be useful when you have no messaging debt.

5. You aren’t deleting. You are using unread/read as replacements for unfinished/finished. The only place where we remove messages is email (archive to preserve search).

Now, app by app strategies:

iMessage/Signal:

Always first priority, read & respond instantly. Priority not because high signal but because you can’t apply any inbox mgmt strategies.

Email:

1. Your inbox is a todo list

2. Read all emails as they come in (but don't reply)

3. Archive anything you don’t need to respond to
4. Use "skip it and archive" filtering for frequent messages (in Gmail, search bar for sender or subject, create a filter rule)

5. Unsubscribe from every newsletter as it comes in. If this isn’t working, you can create a filter. But you need to progressively eliminate spam as a high priority

6. When ready to reply on desktop, hit archive. Keep your inbox clean

Slack:

1. In order to clear: click groups with no mentions but don’t read, read & respond to groups with mentions

2.  Mute all groups with > 20, you can read on a Saturday if you want

3. Unread DMs, long hold and preview before reading. If easy, respond on phone. If not, leave and respond at desktop

Telegram/Whatsapp:

1. Two folders, Unread, and All

2. Mute all groups

3. In order: click in and out of groups with no mentions, then read and respond to groups with mentions

4. Handle DMs last, long hold and preview first. If instant, respond on phone. If not, leave and respond later.

5. Leave groups aggressively, don’t join any channels or social chats > 20 people. If you find yourself in one, leave.

X/LinkedIn/Instagram/etc.

1. Allow message requests from verified users

2. A lot of spam but can apply read/unread strategy

3. Read all to get started

I know this is lengthy but once you get the basics, you will build a new mental model of how to deal with messages from everywhere.

And you will soon have empty inboxes everywhere, allowing you to reply to new ones with tremendous speed.

text:
Bubbles are made of multiples. This market is made of earnings. a16z's David George and Santiago Rodriguez on what makes this cycle different from 2000 or 2021:

David: "The market has reached new highs, and at the same time that it has reached new highs, the trading multiples of the market are actually down."

"Stocks are up about 20% while multiples are down about 20%. What that means is the performance is driven by fundamental earnings, not increased multiples."

"It's nothing like the dot-com boom, where some of the highest market cap companies in the world had their massive stock run-ups based on increases in their trading multiples and would trade, in many cases, for like 100x PE. That's not what's happening here."

Santiago: "Since ChatGPT came out almost four years ago, the market's up 90%, which is 17% annualized."

"Any time there's been a 17% annualized growth for four years, the natural instinct is, well, that's got to come down."

"But when you compare that to the market trading for below 20x earnings growing 15%, this definitely feels a little different than the 2021 period or the 2000 period, when multiples and growth were not really going together."

author: a16z
quoted_text:
a16z's David George, Sarah Wang, Alex Immerman, and Santiago Rodriguez on the State of Markets, from AI and infrastructure to the next investment cycles:

1. Tech is the everything cycle.

High-tech equipment, software, and R&D are now about 55% of US capital spending, and the AI buildout just passed the railroads as a share of GDP. The five largest hyperscalers will spend about $780B on capex this year, heading past $1T in 2027, and demand still outstrips supply at every point in the chain.

2. It's an earnings story.

Stocks are up about 20% while multiples are down about 20%, and the S&P trades under 20x earnings. The market is up 90% since ChatGPT, on 15% earnings growth.

3. AI adoption is broad and shallow.

69% of the S&P 500 has a live AI deployment, 30% report a quantified result, and just 2% have AI doing a job they'd notice if it stopped. The power users are pulling away: the top 1% of AI spenders spend eight times the top 10%.

4. The private markets are enormous.

Six private companies, Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, and Revolut, add up to about $2.4T by last round, more than every IPO of the past decade combined. "The founder is the asset class. The IPO is another financing event."

Plus: why a data center can lower your electricity bill, what Amazon saying no to Muse and Instacart saying yes tells you about marketplaces, and the seven areas the team is most excited about next.

Google just dropped new model with some crazy benchmarks. Weeks before the Anthropic IPO. This whole macro is popcorn 🍿 and tiresome like streaming subs

How is Anthropic going to compete with Google’s distribution?

How are they going to compete with AWS / GCP on  inference for enterprise?

How are they going to compete with open-weight models on the work that does not require high intelligence like OCR, data extraction, reading numbers from one doc and writing them into another? That is honestly like 70% of agentic work.

How are they going to compete when data collection is outsourced to vendors?

The only thing they really have is training. And training produces a snapshot. A one-time, static model.

So they need to invent things like continuous training. And they need to stretch that category as far as it can go, even place training pieces at the customer like LoRa.

I would heavily acquire the data providers. That is the only real place of safety. Own the data ingestion channels. The more, the better
