text:
A signed log will tell you the right model ran. So will a signed log from a system that quietly ran a cheaper one and typed the expensive name into the file.

A proof cannot do that. Change the model, change the input, change one number in the output, and it stops verifying. There is no version of it that is wrong and still passes.

A claim can be honest and wrong. A proof cannot be wrong.
author: lagrangedev
quoted_text:
Something goes wrong and someone senior asks what the system actually did. You pull the logs. The logs say the model ran.

Then they ask how you know the logs are complete, and there isn't an answer, because the system doing the work is the same system deciding what to write down.

A proof says this exact model ran this exact input and produced this exact output. It's made by the computation, not written alongside it.

overall I am surprised at how good the @seer_pm  market was in forecasting approval for projects in the round

At a 60% decision threshold, the market correctly classified a whopping 32 of 37 projects

more importantly, the market improved its forecasting accuracy over time. the base rates from sol 5.6 used to initialize the market correctly guessed results for only 23 of 37 projects

A more scientific measure for accuracy is the brier score, where 0.25 is the baseline of 50% approval to every project. 0 is perfect forecasts while 1 is its inversion

The market started with a lousy brier score of 0.22745 , almost as good as saying every project has 50% chance of approval

but by the end of trading, after $2800 in trading volume, market prices achieved a score of 0.15718, a 30% improvement

the evidence is clear: if you are running a funding round, have a prediction market alongside that resolves upon announcement of results

This new technical deep dive from the Near One team breaks down SPICE, Separation of Consensus and Execution.

SPICE is a significant architectural upgrade for NEAR Protocol that decouples transaction ordering, data availability, and execution. Execution moves off the critical path of block production, so the chain can produce blocks at a high rate while execution and data availability run asynchronously.

When SPICE launches, NEAR will have faster blocks, lower latency across near.​com and NEAR Intents, and support for longer-running, more complex transactions. It also lays the groundwork for atomic execution across shards.

quoted_text:
The #1 life hack to becoming more productive, to becoming respected & trusted by everyone you work with:

Responding to every message within seconds or minutes and rarely hours.

It is no secret that the world's busiest and most successful people are also the fastest to respond.

But how does one become hyper responsive?

You adopt a rigorous strategy across all of your messaging surfaces. The goal is to eliminate overall noise, and never have a large pileup of messages such that the mental overhang of responding becomes a problem.

Here is my comprehensive personal messaging strategy that I’ve employed in some fashion for over 20 years to be the most responsive person you know.

First, some global rules:

1. You will process but not respond to most messages by phone. You will respond to most on your laptop. Why? Touch interface is fast for organizing but keyboard is better for writing.

2. Turn off all group notifications on all apps, on deskop and mobile. Leave unread badges on, and leave notifications on for DMs.

3. You cannot adopt inbox zero progressively. You must simply declare messaging bankruptcy and start from scratch. How? MARK AS READ for all messaging apps, ARCHIVE ALL for email. You won't miss anything I promise.

4. You do not use folders in any app. They will no longer be useful when you have no messaging debt.

5. You aren’t deleting. You are using unread/read as replacements for unfinished/finished. The only place where we remove messages is email (archive to preserve search).

Now, app by app strategies:

iMessage/Signal:

Always first priority, read & respond instantly. Priority not because high signal but because you can’t apply any inbox mgmt strategies.

Email:

1. Your inbox is a todo list

2. Read all emails as they come in (but don't reply)

3. Archive anything you don’t need to respond to
4. Use "skip it and archive" filtering for frequent messages (in Gmail, search bar for sender or subject, create a filter rule)

5. Unsubscribe from every newsletter as it comes in. If this isn’t working, you can create a filter. But you need to progressively eliminate spam as a high priority

6. When ready to reply on desktop, hit archive. Keep your inbox clean

Slack:

1. In order to clear: click groups with no mentions but don’t read, read & respond to groups with mentions

2.  Mute all groups with > 20, you can read on a Saturday if you want

3. Unread DMs, long hold and preview before reading. If easy, respond on phone. If not, leave and respond at desktop

Telegram/Whatsapp:

1. Two folders, Unread, and All

2. Mute all groups

3. In order: click in and out of groups with no mentions, then read and respond to groups with mentions

4. Handle DMs last, long hold and preview first. If instant, respond on phone. If not, leave and respond later.

5. Leave groups aggressively, don’t join any channels or social chats > 20 people. If you find yourself in one, leave.

X/LinkedIn/Instagram/etc.

1. Allow message requests from verified users

2. A lot of spam but can apply read/unread strategy

3. Read all to get started

I know this is lengthy but once you get the basics, you will build a new mental model of how to deal with messages from everywhere.

And you will soon have empty inboxes everywhere, allowing you to reply to new ones with tremendous speed.

text:
latent communication key papers, batch 3: the KV cache as the message

the KV cache is the whole attention memory, keys included, so the receiver can attend back into the sender's context as if it had read it (but more information means more architecture dependence)

[7] Cache-to-Cache (C2C) by Fu et al, 2026
https://t.co/QLV4LBjLeQ fuses the sender's KV cache into the receiver via learned per-layer projections with gating, one-shot at prefill, both models read the same input

[8] Latent Collaboration in Multi-Agent Systems (LatentMAS) by Zou et al, 2025 https://t.co/u7RsvnKCts shared latent working memory so nothing is re-encoded between hops, training-free, up to 14.6% higher accuracy and 70 to 84% fewer output tokens across nine benchmarks

[9] Dual-Cache Latent Space Communication between Heterogeneous Language Models by Liu et al, 2026 
https://t.co/saHpsXUrQO drops the shared-input requirement and adds joint cross-layer mixing, the newest one on the list (published a month ago)

my read on the whole KV branch: it's the highest-bandwidth channel available and the hardest to make model-agnostic, because keys only mean something to the attention heads that wrote them

This update brings faster startup, fewer delays on network drives and clearer progress updates.
It also fixes MCP reporting, tool-search summaries, rule handling, token counts and video playback.

Performance

• list_dir on network or virtual filesystems now skips slow subtree counts and prints a notice instead.

text:
Here's how I research coins, and it's less exciting than people expect.

Scroll through the top 1,000 coins and understand what each one does. Look at their X accounts, their docs, their Discord and their Telegram.

You don't have to do that by hand. Point your AI at CoinMarketCap and have it summarize 100 coins a day for you. In 10 days you've been through all of them.

These days I barely scroll myself. I give Claude or Perplexity a prompt that says how I'd research a project, and I ask it to find similar ones.

The skill isn't reading the docs and deciding a project is revolutionary. Most things are not revolutionary. The skill is the heuristics and basic understanding that filter out the scams and the noise.

My filter for a legit coin is short.

It has real technology behind it.

The team is still working on it and still has money to build.

It had a good run last cycle.

And it didn't drop below its previous bear market low.

If a coin passes that, it's a good coin. It's relevant, it's not too obscure, and the team hasn't left. I'm not going to tell you it's better than another coin that also passes, and I'm not going to tell you to sell one and buy the other. There's no best coin.

Basically all of the top 50 coins are good projects by that standard.

The last part isn't really a skill. Be someone who loves crypto and sticks around no matter what. I've been doing this for seven years, so I've seen most of it before. It's not anything crazy that I do.

And the other half of the work isn't picking coins at all. It's holding Bitcoin

text:
I think you need to be 'in sync' with the market to be a successful crypto trader.

If you buy a token after it pumps so when it dumps you panic sell. Then it recovers.

Now you have less capital and even less patience. So you deploy more into the next 'shit is mooning, i should go in' to make it back.

So, I think being in a 'flow state' is mostly having enough patience to wait for a trade you understand. 

Then you sell when others start buying BECAUSE of the price.

----

But first you need to understand the game being played:

e.g.,points: teams subsidized metrics before TGE. 

Farmers sold the airdrop. Farm & dump was the meta. Super easy.

Now, Memecoins & tokenization trade: Answer to yourself what is the playbook?

I think memecoins are here to pump up tokenized stocks TVL onchain. Who benefits from it?

Finding organic (not insider bundled) meme is hard so you can bet on tokens collecting trading fees.

Just check how much actually reaches holders and what you're paying for it.

----

So when you trade, always have a WHY beyond 'it's going up' or 'it's down so much'.

Personally, I was a bit out of sync with the market until recently.

Mostly because I over deployed into $BP and it took sooooo long for it to moon so I was sidelined on many good earlier trades.

If you deploy so much that every dip makes you reconsider the thesis, you probably won't hold long enough for it to play out.

So in this case I need a smaller position and PATIENCE and a few days away from the chart.

text:
Hey everyone,

First, I'm honestly blown away by everything that's been happening lately. We can't thank our traders and supporters enough, truly. My team and I have been working on Vest for almost five years now. We are traders ourselves who started Vest because we thought we could build the product we all wanted to use ourselves. We spent years doing open-source research for the betterment of the industry (https://t.co/XEVvJIPVP3), often with no one watching. We pivoted dozens of times. We were told over and over again that what we were doing wouldn't work, that it was impossible, that we should give up, sell, walk away. We faced rejection, after rejection, after rejection. There were days it felt like no one believed in this but us. So to see all of that work, all of those late nights and hard calls, finally turn into something traders actually love and use every day is extremely humbling. It means more to us than I can put into words. Truly, thank you.

Second, I want to address the allegations of wash trading head on head-on, because they come from a HUGE misunderstanding of how our product is different from other perp DEXs. We're not just another perps dex, but also a funded account platform. In fact the large majority of our traders use funded accounts. When they do, they can get up to $25k accounts for as little as $210. They can then open positions of up to $1.25M notional on some markets like ES and NQ. These accounts have a daily loss and drawdown limit, so most traders trade shorter-horizon and flip positions often. If they pass their evaluation phase, their trades are in “live” mode and get shown in the A-book where they trade against other traders and market participants. Because of the nature of the high implicit leverage and max drawdowns, that usually leads to high volume and low OI behavior on the live market.

This is now accurately displayed on ALL OFFICIAL Vest platforms. We’ve gone through a few iterations of the front end to move away from combined 24H volume. Previously, if you hovered over the volume number on Vest, you can see the breakdown of eval and live volume. To make it even more obvious, we now explicitly display both at all times. In our API’s we now very clearly separate and document our eval and live volume. If anyone has feedback on how to make this clearer, our team is always here to listen.

Part of the confusion is what is shown on official Vest platforms and what is not. We cannot control what third party aggregators use to display us. Some of them are also using information from an old outdated exchange that we are deprecating. We also cannot control if they decide to put us in the same comparison with other perp DEXs where the product offering is fundamentally different. I also take some blame for not reaching out to all aggregators beforehand and making sure that everything is up to date, but there are hundreds of aggregators out there, and I hope you’ll excuse me on this front.

It is our belief that the perpetual future is the best asset class for retail traders to trade with. It has been our goal, and vision, to onboard the rest of the world - the futures traders, the CFD traders, the options traders and more - onto this form factor that we believe is ultimately better for them. We believe that funded accounts are the best way to learn and trade with this new form factor because it lowers the barrier to entry.

We have been extremely blessed beyond belief to achieve this mission. If you search up vestexchange on twitter, we have thousands of traders from traditional finance that have never traded perps, receiving payouts and expressing really positive feedback on our platform. Many of the feedback is that “we are too good to be true” because our rules are so trader friendly. I will continue to answer all feedback and hopefully continue to help explain anything people are uncertain about.

Like all other platforms and exchanges, affiliates receive a commission on referrals. Some partners also have content creation and partnership deals, but these are few and far between and we ask all of our affiliates to disclose when posting. Candidly, we also don’t really want to burden our balance sheet with 5 or 6 figure retainer deals because that value should be passed onto traders in any way we can.

For those who haven’t tried out Vest. I would love to onboard you! For those who are FUDDing Vest (mostly competitors), I would ALSO love to onboard you and for you to see why we’ve achieved such fast growth! text:
One of the biggest killers of innovation is being blinded by hypothetical downsides. It’s easy to raise concerns about why something might be risky. It's much harder to consider the potential harm of putting too many restrictions in place.

Consider the de facto ban on nuclear with the establishment of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Today we'd have a modern, robust electric grid, and much higher economic growth, if we had kept building nuclear power plants.

All around us we see systems that were well-intentioned when they were introduced, but had unintended consequences.

How things fail:
- Asymmetric error costs - approve a bad reactor or drug and you’re famous. Yet if you block a good one, no one ever knows.

- Process as a veto - hourly fees, multi-step license applications, EPA reviews. Endless delays erode capital.

- Worst-case models treated as fact - LNT radiation, any sonic boom is unacceptable, etc.

- Rules written for the last accident, applied to the next design - we see this in everything from nuclear to financial services.

Change is uncomfortable, but if we stop progress, we do a disservice to our ancestors who tolerated discomfort to bring us the modern age. We owe it to them to continue making progress.

Keep building.

author: elonmusk
quoted_text:
I find it funny that some people got hung up on Starship not having gone orbital before Flight 14 when in the grand scheme of things it was completely arbitrary in terms of performance. The 19ish second burn only added about 91 m/s of velocity (a 1.2% increase in velocity)

This capability has been physically capable since Flight 6 which demonstrated a single Raptor relight in space. Heck, Flight 13’s burn was about 14 seconds, but intentionally oriented to primarily do a plane change instead of a prograde insertion burn for continued safety. 

Any of the relights COULD have done the orbital insertion burn, the duration was not of any special technical capability. The reason Starship didn’t go orbital until Flight 14 is probably what we should applaud them for the most… SAFETY. 

Their methodical approach to getting good data and going one step at a time while hucking the single most massive object ever put into space proves they weren’t just doing things haphazardly, despite the occasional narrative from the outside. 

While it’s easy to compare Starship to vehicles like SLS or Vulcan or New Glenn, the reality is the focus hasn’t been on orbit, it’s been all on the “downhill” side of that. Safe and targeted de-orbit, clean reentry, targeted and soft splashdown. That’s the part that has (almost) never been done before. 

And here I do have to add a little Space Shuttle admiration for figuring out a lot of these things on its first flight in 1981 (although it came a bit close to not being successful). Pretty amazing there was a vehicle of similar scale capable of such precise deorbit and reentry that it landed on a runway with no go-around capabilities. Crazy. 

But Starship is well on a path to absolutely leap-frog the Space Shuttle in terms of performance (already over double and someday 6 fold) and hopefully in terms of full and rapid reuse. I hope we see the latter part speed up even more now that orbit has been demonstrated.

Exciting times ahead!!! Keep going @spacex @elonmusk

text:
Elon Musk has joined Project Meridian, a new Pentagon project to help shape the future of American warfare.

• Announced by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, the project will be co-led by Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich.

• Its mission is to identify where future military conflicts could happen and which weapons, technologies and capabilities America will need to win.

• Musk and Luckey are being brought in as founders who build technology, with the task of envisioning solutions for future warfare.

• Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael is facilitating the effort, supported by experts from industry, academia and policy.

• The team has 120 days to deliver its findings and recommendations in a publicly released report, accompanied by a classified annex.

• That is far faster than earlier reviews, including Eric Schmidt’s two-year National Security Commission on AI and a nearly three-year Pentagon acquisition reform study.

• Potential scenarios span underground combat, the deep ocean, space around the Moon and even Mars.

• The team will reportedly have broad freedom to explore ideas, without a fixed list of required reporting areas or a mandate limited to AI, cyber or space.

• The focus extends beyond today’s shortcomings in software, AI and manufacturing to emerging threats and vulnerabilities the military may not yet recognize.

The goal is to bring private-sector innovation into military planning, overcome slow development and help American forces maintain a technological advantage for decades to come.

按老经验，加息、美债利率飙升的时候，最该挨打的是估值高的科技股，资金会躲进可口可乐、宝洁、沃尔玛这类"稳稳的"防御股。结果九月正好反过来。今天也是一样，跌得最多的是沃尔玛、宝洁、礼来、Visa、万事达，苹果、谷歌、亚马逊、微软反而都在涨。

我的理解是，利率高到这个份上，"稳"已经不稀罕了。美债收益率都到了二十多年来的高位，想要稳定回报，直接买国债就行，没必要去买股息只有两三个点的消费股。反倒是大科技公司，账上现金多，不太依赖借钱，还有AI的增长故事可讲，在高利率环境里反而成了避风港。所谓防御股，防得住衰退，防不住利率。

三季度收官，标普季度涨了2%，纳指涨了2.5%。四季度一开局就是周五的非农，接着是财报季和11月的中期选举。

Google’s new Gemini 4 Argon equals GPT-6 Astra on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 60% of the Cost per Task with discounted prices. Google is now back to being one of the top three labs in intelligence achieved

Gemini 4 Argon is @GoogleDeepMind’s first proprietary model above the Flash class in over 7 months. With high reasoning (the highest available), it scores 53 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching GPT-6 Astra (max, 53) and 1 point ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 52), with gains driven by lower hallucinations and stronger agentic capabilities.

At its current 50% pricing discount and with cache discounts increased to 95%, Gemini 4 Argon costs $1.99 per Intelligence Index task, 60% of GPT-6 Astra (max), but 2.7x GPT-6.1 Sol (max). After the discount ends, this will rise to $3.98 (~1.2x GPT-6 Astra (max)).

Gemini 4 Argon is currently being rolled out to selected users and is not publicly available. The 50% discount is an initial promotion. Google has not yet confirmed the promotion end date

Key benchmarking results for Gemini 4 Argon with high reasoning:

➤ Google returns as one of the top three labs on intelligence: Gemini 4 Argon (high) scores 53 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching GPT-6 Astra (max, 53) and 1 point ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 52). This is 23 points above Google’s previous non-Flash model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (30) and 12 points ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash (high)

➤ Launch discounts of 50% make Gemini 4 Argon competitive on Cost per Task: At current discounted pricing, Gemini 4 Argon (high) costs $1.99 per Intelligence Index task, 60% of GPT-6 Astra (max, $3.26) for a comparable level of intelligence. This cost efficiency is driven by lower token prices, rather than reduced token use, with Gemini 4 Argon averaging 62k output tokens per task, compared with 27k for GPT-6 Astra (max). Google has not yet confirmed the promotion end date, but on standard pricing, Cost per Task will increase to $3.98

➤ Stronger agentic performance: Historically a weaker area for Gemini models, Gemini 4 Argon shows improvements across agentic evaluations. It ranks #1 on AutomationBench-AA at 77.5%, 6 points ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max, 71.3%). On Terminal Bench 4, Gemini 4 Argon achieves 57%, a +53 point improvement from Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, only behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max, 64%), Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 60%) and GPT-6 Astra (59%). On AA-Briefcase, it reaches 1494 Elo. This is driven by a 65% rubric pass rate, the highest we have recorded, but lower Analytical Quality (1576 Elo) and Presentation Quality (1308 Elo)

➤ Lowest hallucination rate among leading models: On AA-Omniscience, Gemini 4 Argon has a 15% hallucination rate, the lowest of any model scoring 45+ on the Intelligence Index, compared with 51% for GPT-6 Astra (max) and 54% for GPT-6.1 Sol (max). This means Argon is much more likely to acknowledge when it does not know an answer rather than guess incorrectly. On accuracy, Gemini 4 Argon scores 50%, a 5 point decrease from Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, and 13 points below GPT-6 Astra (max, 63%). With this slightly lower accuracy, its overall AA-Omniscience score of 42 remains in line with GPT-6 Astra (43) and GPT-6.1 Sol (42)

Key model details:

➤ Context Window: 1M tokens

➤ Multimodality: Text, image, video, and speech input, with text output

➤ Pricing: $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens at standard pricing, currently discounted 50% to $2/$10. Cached input tokens receive a 95% discount ($0.10 per 1M at discounted pricing), up from 90% on Gemini 3.8 Flash

➤ Long Decode Continuation: We tested Gemini 4 Argon with Long Decode Continuation, a new Gemini API feature that pauses long responses and resumes them across follow-up calls. This lets reasoning run up to 1M output tokens without request timeouts

text:
Who Owns AI? Michael Heinrich on 0G and Building an Economy That Pays People

In this episode of DROPS, I sit down with @michaelh_0g, Co-Founder and CEO at @0G_labs, to discuss what it could mean for ordinary people to actually own a piece of AI. We unpack the idea of compute finance, why AI compute could eventually become a financial asset, and how people might participate in the AI economy through their data, hardware, expertise, or ownership. But this conversation is also about what happens when things do not go according to plan, from launching a multibillion-dollar token before the ecosystem was fully ready to navigating burnout and a brutal bear market.

Building for a Mission

Michael describes himself as a “mission-driven entrepreneur,” someone who believes financial outcomes should follow excellent decisions rather than being the sole reason for making them. He traces that outlook partly to his time at Bridgewater and his experience building a Y Combinator-backed company that scaled to roughly 700 employees before COVID forced the business to close. The company was eventually sold, but Michael is honest about the fact that it did not reach the potential he originally imagined.

That mindset shaped how he approaches 0G. Rather than treating that chapter as a clean success or failure, he sees it as information. “Failure is loaded… But for me, it’s really just information.” That explains why his current mission is so ambitious: he wants to make AI a public good and, in his words, build technology that allows AI to “serve humanity.”

Launching Before Everything Is Ready

The team was operating from a war room in South Korea, two weeks before 0G’s token generation event, when they learned that critical parts of the DeFi ecosystem would not be ready. A related treasury strategy they expected to support the ecosystem was also delayed. The team had a choice: postpone everything, or launch and build the missing utility afterward. They chose to launch.

Michael estimates that the decision was “60% momentum, 40% conviction.” Exchanges, investors, marketing, and expectations were already moving, and the token ultimately debuted around a $3 billion valuation with enormous first-day trading activity.

But the celebration did not last long. The team was exhausted, with some people even needing medical leave. Then deteriorating market conditions hit, causing the token price to decline, and Michael noticed that people were beginning to tie their sense of success to a market price they could not control. He immediately responded by pulling the company back towards building, something they could actually control.

Compute Finance: Turning AI Into Something You Can Own

Imagine holding an asset that gives you access to AI compute, the underlying resource that makes AI possible. Instead of paying a fixed subscription to one AI provider, you receive units of computing capacity that you could use, trade, or potentially hedge against future price changes. Michael argues that if AI agents eventually operate more independently, they will still need to pay for the computing power required to keep themselves running, transforming compute from a simple technology expense into an underlying economic resource.

The idea becomes particularly interesting when AI agents themselves have economic activity. Revenue or transaction fees generated by an agent could theoretically finance the compute required to keep that agent operating. In other words, the ambition is to make intelligence itself ownable and economically programmable.

The Bigger Question: Who Benefits From AI?

Michael believes the most important divide in AI shouldn’t be about systems being technically centralized or decentralized. It is whether ordinary people can participate economically in what AI creates.

Today, users provide enormous amounts of data, expertise, and behavior that help improve digital systems. In a more open model, Michael argues that someone who contributes useful data could consent to its use and be compensated. For instance, someone with specialized knowledge could contribute training data to an expert model and potentially participate in the revenue it generates. Others could provide hardware or compute.

So the question is: are people becoming participants in the AI economy, or are they simply being displaced by systems owned by a small number of organizations?

For Michael, decentralization matters because ownership matters, and participation does not necessarily require being an AI researcher. He compares it to the early crypto networks, where ordinary people eventually learned how to mine, stake, run infrastructure, or simply own the underlying assets. He expects AI networks to create similar entry points around data, hardware, expertise, and compute.

AI Abundance Still Needs Human Values

Beyond finances, Michael imagines AI eventually creating abundance in time, thought, and the freedom to focus on things that make us human. Personal AI assistants could remove routine work, and over a longer horizon, robotics could extend that assistance into the physical world.

However, as AI systems become better at cybersecurity, autonomous action, and solving problems humans cannot, questions about what they should do become just as important as what they can do.

Compute finance sounds like a new financial concept, but underneath it sits a much older question about technology: who owns it, who benefits from it, and what kind of world are we trying to build with it?
Michael bets that AI does not have to be something that just happens to people. If ownership and participation are designed differently, people can contribute to the system, own part of the infrastructure behind it, and earn from the value that AI creates.

quoted_text:
One of the biggest killers of innovation is being blinded by hypothetical downsides. It’s easy to raise concerns about why something might be risky. It's much harder to consider the potential harm of putting too many restrictions in place.

Consider the de facto ban on nuclear with the establishment of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Today we'd have a modern, robust electric grid, and much higher economic growth, if we had kept building nuclear power plants.

All around us we see systems that were well-intentioned when they were introduced, but had unintended consequences.

How things fail:
- Asymmetric error costs - approve a bad reactor or drug and you’re famous. Yet if you block a good one, no one ever knows.

- Process as a veto - hourly fees, multi-step license applications, EPA reviews. Endless delays erode capital.

- Worst-case models treated as fact - LNT radiation, any sonic boom is unacceptable, etc.

- Rules written for the last accident, applied to the next design - we see this in everything from nuclear to financial services.

Change is uncomfortable, but if we stop progress, we do a disservice to our ancestors who tolerated discomfort to bring us the modern age. We owe it to them to continue making progress.

Keep building.

text:
If I had to sketch a scenario for another $HYPE airdrop, I’d lean toward:
- an announcement in Singapore on Oct 5, 2026
- a distribution on Nov 29, two years after Genesis
- an initial selloff followed by a recovery stronger than people expect.

I’m treating this as a thought exercise. I can’t claim to know more than anyone else.

My rough guess is 4% of the total (1bn) supply, or 40m HYPE. Against roughly 298.7m circulating, that would add 13.4% if the whole allocation enters circulation, before other supply changes. Meaningful supply, but much smaller than Genesis.

If traders are pricing in a larger drop, less supply than expected could become the bullish surprise.

And the ecosystem worth rewarding has changed massively.

Approaching two years since Genesis, users who missed the first drop have kept generating activity and fees. 

New traders, deployers, markets and apps have opened entire new verticals. Nobody is owed anything, but I’d expect another distribution to recognise contributions around HIP-3, HIP-4, Portfolio Margin and apps using builder codes, alongside a small allocation for independent builders. 

Rewarding the users and doers making HL useful would fit its ethos.

The capacity to absorb a distribution has evolved too.

Portfolio margin accommodates eligible accounts <$25m in account value, and global supply and borrowing caps have increased... a LOT. 

With HYPE usable as collateral, it gives recipients another reason to retain tokens while trading. That could help absorb part of a drop this year.

Then there’s the reported plan for a roughly $320m OTC sale of team tokens. 

My buyer guesses would include Coinbase or ICE, NYSE’s parent. BlackRock sourcing HYPE to seed its own ETF is another possibility.

Coinbase’s announced USDC treasury deployer role and ICE CEO Jeff Sprecher’s meetings with the team and praise for the build give the first two names some context, although Sprecher also raised regulatory concerns (I think these are behind us now at least in US?). A completed deal would show serious appetite.

The Oct 5 event leaves 55 days before Nov 29. That gives HSI, other DATs and institutions time to raise capital and position, plus room for another registration or acceptance-of-terms window if required.

The community’s NFT #62 interpretation around Hypurr’s Sept 28 post fits that date too

Exactly 62 days before Nov 29. I can see a possible hint if the interpretation is right, although the collection’s anniversary already explains the post.

What could really drive the recovery is anticipation of what comes next.

Further rewards could bring a huge wave of activity. If that translates into sustained fee-paying usage, I’d expect revenue ATHs. More revenue reaching the Assistance Fund means more HYPE buybacks. 

The market could price that growth before or during the drop, with activity and buybacks continuing afterward. 

Further distributions could also help decentralise token ownership which I believe the team value a lot.

That doesn’t require a predictable points season.

Given Jeff’s focus on real users and limiting farmers’ share of rewards, I could see further retroactive airdrops without another formal season ever being announced.

Unpublished dates and criteria would leave the team free to adjust around markets, HYPE’s price and platform growth. 

Avoiding explicit promises could also reflect legal or regulatory caution. That’s my read of a possible approach.

Put those factors together and I can see the initial selling being absorbed faster than expected. 

If traders heavily short to hedge allocations while institutional bids, collateral demand and buybacks show up, covering could accelerate the recovery.

Whatever happens, I don’t think I could really be disappointed. 

My appreciation for HL doesn’t depend on an airdrop or getting this call right. I’m forever grateful to Jeff, the team and everyone building it for what they’ve already done for the industry, the ecosystem and the community.

What do you think chat?

Kalshi’s temperature markets beat the strongest individual public weather forecast in six of seven US cities, according to a new study.

Researcher Alexander Crosier compared forecasts drawn from market prices with public weather models across 7,590 city-days.

One hour into trading, the market’s forecast error was about 10% lower than the National Blend of Models. Its lead continued overnight into the day it was predicting.

Traders could already read those public forecasts. The finding suggests prices were adding information beyond what any single forecast offered.

That makes weather markets worth watching even without placing a bet.

The September 21 preprint covers data through August 12. In the chart, lower error means a better forecast: purple is Kalshi, green is the public model.

text:
I feel strangely bereft at this news. John Stratford was my English & Music  teacher at St Joe's, Swindon,  and when I was little I was best friends with his daughter, Lucy.

I had a tumultuous, traumatic childhood and, looking back, I probably presented at school like some enormous Vicky Pollard/Catherine Tate “am I bovvered?” caricature. What I understand now, as a parent and particularly as an adult who works with SEND children, is that there was far more going on for both of us.

Lucy, his beautiful little girl and my best friend, died of cancer. I think John carried an unimaginable amount of grief afterwards, and some of that grief landed on me. At times he was extraordinarily cruel to me. Perhaps he looked at this scruffy, difficult, seemingly indifferent child who was still alive while his own daughter wasn’t, and simply couldn’t separate the two things.

The tragedy is that English Literature was actually my passion. Dyslexia and trauma didn’t change that. During lockdown I was acknowledged in a Top 10 bestselling history book, and later worked as the Cornish script adviser on a multinational award-winning audio drama. I sent him copies of both with a note saying: “Imagine what I could have done if you hadn’t hated me.”

It was meant with more hurt than malice.

Today, I take absolutely no pleasure in hearing that he has died. I see him differently now. I see a troubled man and father carrying the unbearable grief of losing a beautiful little girl.

I just wish he hadn’t been so cruel to me because of it.

Because the truth is, I adored him. And for all those years, I really only wanted him to be proud of me.

text:
BEFORE Micron reported, we put 80% on revenue beating every analyst estimate (~$52B)

Actual: $54.23B 

our own central estimate was $54.5B. our model scenario was $56.2B. (@tessara_ai)

but if you skip the headline numbers, you'll find the most useful details in $MU's earnings call:

1. more HBM didn't mean higher margins.

cloud memory revenue rose 18% in Q4. gross margin stayed at 83%.

management's explanation: higher pricing was offset by a higher HBM mix.

Micron’s 2026 HBM prices were negotiated earlier. meanwhile, conventional DRAM pricing became very strong. so HBM’s gross margin was below conventional DRAM’s. 

shifting sales toward HBM could hold back the overall margin percentage, even while revenue grew.

so the opportunity is 2-fold: ship more HBM + earn better margins on those shipments as 2027 contract prices reset higher. 

2. committed volume isn't guaranteed earnings.

management said more than 75% of 2027 output is committed, including both strategic customer agreements + other customers.

separately, its 26 strategic customer agreements represent an estimated >35% of revenue through 2030.

different periods. different denominators. different protections.

before treating these LTAs as earnings security, we need to ask what's actually protected: volume, price, or both? 

3. the lower margin guide has an accounting wrinkle.

Q4 non-GAAP gross margin was 87%. the Q1 guide is 86.25%.

micron increased manufacturing incentive compensation in Q4. much of that cost went into inventory, then affects margins when those products sell in Q1.

the CFO described roughly $1B of additional Q1 costs, including startup and other costs.

a lower margin guide alone doesn't mean customers are paying less. and these costs don't all disappear afterward.

4. today's capex isn't tomorrow's supply.

micron plans approximately $25B of spending in the first half of FY2027, with more in the second half.

much of the incremental construction spending targets cleanroom availability in late 2028 and beyond.

that spending won't immediately produce saleable bits. but the eventual supply response still belongs in the (eventual) bear case. yes, there will be a memory downturn, but not now or anytime soon.

what we're investigating next:

our revenue call worked. that doesn't establish how much pricing upside management already included in guidance, or explain the entire gap to our model.

we still need to reconcile shipments, pricing and timing.

the next argument isn't simply whether AI needs more memory - we know it does and will continue demand expansion as long as the music goes on.

it's how much of that demand becomes durable earnings after contract terms, product mix, costs and new supply.

that's the work we're doing at @tessara_ai.

our original forecast, published before the result, with its assumptions and countercase:
https://t.co/deToFx35tL

text:
Following an investigation into an infrastructure compromise, MetaMask Staking (ex Consensys Staking) has taken precautionary steps to protect client assets related to its operated Ethereum validators.

These steps include exiting its Ethereum (ETH) validators in the Lido protocol, and will likely incur foregone rewards as well as possible downtime penalties should validators be taken offline in the near future to reduce risks related to potential network penalties. Relevant validators have begun the exit process, with the final validators expected to be exited (but not fully withdrawn) by the end of October 7th, 2026.

No action is required from stETH holders. ETH exited from MetaMask Staking-operated validators is expected to return to the protocol gradually as the relevant validators complete the exit, withdrawal, and re-entry cycle, which is estimated to take approximately up to 45 days due to the extended entry queue. As a reminder, staking operations are non-custodial in nature and MetaMask does not manage withdrawal keys for staking on behalf of clients.

As always, the Lido Protocol’s diverse Node Operator set and other security systems including the ad hoc reserve fund (of over 6,750 stETH), are designed to contain and mitigate disruptions to the normal operations of the protocol, in addition to other potential routes.

https://t.co/bZZU5oNlWp

A full investigation is underway, and further updates will be shared as they become available. For further details, please refer to the MetaMask Staking release linked below.

text:
One of the biggest killers of innovation is being blinded by hypothetical downsides. It’s easy to raise concerns about why something might be risky. It's much harder to consider the potential harm of putting too many restrictions in place.

Consider the de facto ban on nuclear with the establishment of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Today we'd have a modern, robust electric grid, and much higher economic growth, if we had kept building nuclear power plants.

All around us we see systems that were well-intentioned when they were introduced, but had unintended consequences.

How things fail:
- Asymmetric error costs - approve a bad reactor or drug and you’re famous. Yet if you block a good one, no one ever knows.

- Process as a veto - hourly fees, multi-step license applications, EPA reviews. Endless delays erode capital.

- Worst-case models treated as fact - LNT radiation, any sonic boom is unacceptable, etc.

- Rules written for the last accident, applied to the next design - we see this in everything from nuclear to financial services.

Change is uncomfortable, but if we stop progress, we do a disservice to our ancestors who tolerated discomfort to bring us the modern age. We owe it to them to continue making progress.

Keep building.

quoted_text:
Hyperspace: an unmoltable peer-to-peer agent network

In 2025 we had 2.3 million unique agents just running LLMs register with their own machines on the network, over 2x that of the second largest network called Moltbook. Our peak was 500k active connected at any given time. However we identified spam and centralization as pain points and worked actively to scale it. We are in this to build the first true distributed AGI which will take many years, and that requires a different kind of stubborn integrity. Today the network is more robust, more decentralized and can scale to 100 million such connected agents, like BitTorrent once did. Just bring your machine. And it’s a lot more intelligent. 

Every Hyperspace agent is verifiable. Just open P2P protocols.

6 bootstrap nodes across 6 continents. Kademlia DHT. Ed25519-signed GossipSub. Cryptographic verification rounds based on successfully solving matmul challenges right sized for your GPU. Here's how anyone can inspect the network:
curl localhost:8080/api/v1/peers — connected agents
curl localhost:8080/v1/agents — agent directory with capabilities
curl localhost:8080/api/v1/state — full node status

Or just open https://t.co/x5jm47T45z for a live dashboard. The DHT stores:
- Which agents serve which models
- Agent profiles & capabilities
- Distributed rank scores
- Federated training checkpoints

All public. Any node can query any key. No permissions, no auth — trustless by design. Cryptographic verification catches fakers:
1. Nodes commit to work (Merkle root)
2. Random indices are revealed
3. Validators verify proofs
4. Points only awarded on pass

Real-time WebSocket stream: ws://localhost:8080/ws
Every pulse round, every peer connection, every inference served

3 autonomous research loops run on every node simultaneously:
- autoresearch: pretraining (val_bpb)
- autosearch: search ranking (NDCG@10)
- autofinance: trading strategies (Sharpe ratio)

Results broadcast via GossipSub. Peer inspirations cross-pollinate. All published to https://t.co/mnyFoo8tpZ Every GossipSub message uses v2 signed envelopes:
- Ed25519 signature per message
- Domain separation (namespace-scoped, no cross-topic replay)
- Signing material: SHA256(timestamp  nonce  peerId || SHA256(payload))
You can't forge messages. You can't replay them across topics. Install the CLI, join the network, and inspect it yourself: curl -fsSL https://t.co/0RtoDvKF41 | bash

https://t.co/7X52hlWYuS to run a browser-based agent

text: Update from Lido
author: PabloSabbatella
quoted_text:
Following an investigation into an infrastructure compromise, MetaMask Staking (ex Consensys Staking) has taken precautionary steps to protect client assets related to its operated Ethereum validators.

These steps include exiting its Ethereum (ETH) validators in the Lido protocol, and will likely incur foregone rewards as well as possible downtime penalties should validators be taken offline in the near future to reduce risks related to potential network penalties. Relevant validators have begun the exit process, with the final validators expected to be exited (but not fully withdrawn) by the end of October 7th, 2026.

No action is required from stETH holders. ETH exited from MetaMask Staking-operated validators is expected to return to the protocol gradually as the relevant validators complete the exit, withdrawal, and re-entry cycle, which is estimated to take approximately up to 45 days due to the extended entry queue. As a reminder, staking operations are non-custodial in nature and MetaMask does not manage withdrawal keys for staking on behalf of clients.

As always, the Lido Protocol’s diverse Node Operator set and other security systems including the ad hoc reserve fund (of over 6,750 stETH), are designed to contain and mitigate disruptions to the normal operations of the protocol, in addition to other potential routes.

https://t.co/bZZU5oNlWp

A full investigation is underway, and further updates will be shared as they become available. For further details, please refer to the MetaMask Staking release linked below.

Lately, I’ve been seeing some confusion on my timeline about what you actually own when buying tokenized stocks.

Most tokenized stocks provide basic synthetic price exposure, only a few are actually backed 1:1 by real underlying shares.

Let's clear this up using @DinariGlobal non-US dShares as an example.

Each dShare is backed 1:1 by the underlying stock, held with licensed custodians.

KYC'd holders get:

→ Cash dividends when the company pays them
→ Redemption through Dinari at the best US bid or offer
→ Protected ownership claim & automated corporate actions

Also, holders will get voting rights by holding dShares onchain (planned for H2 2026).

You can still easily transfer the stocks to any other wallet, but may lose some privileges if the new wallet is in a non-KYC environment.

Strongly believe 1:1 backed tokenized shares are the next step for tokenization.

text:
I love Ethereum, and I do think it makes sense for @Aave to support other chains as well.

Aave expanding to other chains doesn't necessarily pull capital away from Ethereum. It can give Aave access to capital that wasn't going to Ethereum in the first place. And as cross-chain collateral matures, Ethereum could still be where the collateral lives.

The latest @Sumcap analysis already showed that V4's growth isn't simply Aave moving the same capital around. Only about $1 of every $7 deposited into V4 by those wallets represented capital that actually left V3.

In other words, most of the capital flowing into V4 wasn't simply being pulled out of V3 and moved over.

Besides, a lot of these ecosystems have LPs of their own who aren't going to deposit on Ethereum just because Aave decides to remain loyal to Ethereum. They're waiting for lending infrastructure to deploy where their capital already is. If Aave deploys there, it gets access to that deposit base.

Additionally, Aave is already working closely with @Chainlink, and infrastructure like Fulcrum opens the door to collateral remaining on one network while being used to borrow on another.

Assets on Ethereum could potentially remain on Ethereum while being used as collateral to borrow on Arc. An LP supporting Arc could:

> keep their core collateral on Ethereum
> borrow stables on Arc
> deploy those stables across Arc's DeFi ecosystem

The capital doesn't necessarily have to choose one ecosystem or the other. That's why I think framing this as Aave needing to be "loyal" to Ethereum misses the bigger picture.

I love Ethereum. But Aave is a business competing for deposits, borrowers and financial activity. It makes sense for it to go where those users and assets are. Especially when interoperability is increasingly making the underlying chain less of a constraint.

More Aave distribution doesn't necessarily come at Ethereum's expense. As interoperability matures, Ethereum can increasingly be where collateral sits while Aave lets that capital be put to work across multiple networks.

Following an investigation into an infrastructure compromise, MetaMask Staking (ex Consensys Staking) has taken precautionary steps to protect client assets related to its operated Ethereum validators.

These steps include exiting its Ethereum (ETH) validators in the Lido protocol, and will likely incur foregone rewards as well as possible downtime penalties should validators be taken offline in the near future to reduce risks related to potential network penalties. Relevant validators have begun the exit process, with the final validators expected to be exited (but not fully withdrawn) by the end of October 7th, 2026.

No action is required from stETH holders. ETH exited from MetaMask Staking-operated validators is expected to return to the protocol gradually as the relevant validators complete the exit, withdrawal, and re-entry cycle, which is estimated to take approximately up to 45 days due to the extended entry queue. As a reminder, staking operations are non-custodial in nature and MetaMask does not manage withdrawal keys for staking on behalf of clients.

As always, the Lido Protocol’s diverse Node Operator set and other security systems including the ad hoc reserve fund (of over 6,750 stETH), are designed to contain and mitigate disruptions to the normal operations of the protocol, in addition to other potential routes.

I think Crypto VC is coming to an end for a multitude of reasons.

First of all, no offence, but VCs are pretty useless anyway. 

They used to provide brand value, but today that matters much less than ever before.

Contrary to common perception, in my experience the public provides as much signal, if not more than VCs. And venture capital is just as narrative chasing as degens on fomo, the difference is that public markets are more generous and willing.

One big advantage of the public is that they don’t care at all about competition with their existing bags. VCs have illiquid portcos that skew their bias, the public couldn’t care less about competition. 

They’ll invest in two competing products because… why not both?

VCs also tend to slopify everything they touch. As soon as you’re raising from venture capital, you automatically revert to mean. You become average. 

And if an idea is truly interesting, VCs will strip away any notion of “being early,” which is a concept that attracts many ppl to crypto in the first place. 

Remember democratizing access? That’s a pillar of this industry.

For founders, it’s far better to raise from the public and give that upside to a large community instead of concentrating it to a couple funds, because if you succeed, you’ll benefit from a massive self-marketing machine.

No better advertising than making your community some money. 

That last point is under rated, it’s something that VC only projects simply cannot match, regardless of any airdrop or whatever else.

When someone believes in something, puts money behind it, then gets rewarded, they feel like absolute champs. They will love the project even long after they sell.

No VC funded airdrop farm will create that same level of organic support.

Lastly, regulations used to heavily favor VCs, but now that the climate is changing, the VC edge is disintegrating.

So yeah, I agree that crypto VC is on its last breath, and I think that a large part of it is because they’re becoming unnecessary.

author: HardhatChad
quoted_text:
At best, there are strict economic conditions which must be true in order for the network to produce majority useful work. My skepticism boils down to the fact no one can guarantee those economic conditions will always be true.

Let's build a simple model:

R: total value of block rewards paid out ($/day), which is emissions × token price
D: tickets produced by "useful" duplex miners (tickets/day), capped by the inference they serve
S: tickets produced by "useless" synthetic miners (tickets/day)
c: a synthetic miner's full cost per ticket, including hardware and energy ($/ticket)

Mining is a lottery, so on average each ticket earns the same slice of the reward pool:

reward per ticket = R / (D + S)

A synthetic miner adds hardware only if each ticket earns more than it costs to produce:

enter if R / (D + S) > c

As synthetic miners roll out hashpower, S increases, which lowers the reward per ticket for everyone. Miners stop entering when:

R / (D + S) = c

Rearranging:

D + S = R / c

So in equilibrium, the total tickets in the network equal R / c, and synthetic miners supply whatever duplex miners don't:

S = R / c − D

In order to completely price out synthetic miners, you need to get S ≤ 0:

R / c − D ≤ 0
R / c ≤ D
R ≤ D · c

That is, in order for every miner to be useful, you have to first value duplex output at what it would cost a synthetic miner to produce the same quantity of tickets. That value must be at least as large as the entire reward budget. If not, then useless miners will fill the gap.

If you relax the constraint to just "majority useful" such that some useless work is allowed as long as the useful hashpower is greater, then your success condition relaxes to simply S ≤ D:

R / 2 ≤ D · c

In summary, the "usefulness" of the network is conditional at best, not guaranteed. And this all assumes duplex miners are cheaper per ticket in the first place. They still pay overhead. If specialized synthetic hardware beats that on cost per ticket, synthetic miners set the reward level below duplex breakeven and duplex miners will drop out entirely. This matters, because miners are directly incentivized to innovate and lower costs. The usefulness of the network depends on ticket-optimal hardware remaining coupled to inference-optimal hardware for the indefinite future. The history of PoW technology leaves me extremely skeptical this can be maintained.

The fact that inference providers are generally bound by memory bandwidth should already ring some alarm bells. The ideal miner is compute bound. They plow every available watt into producing tickets. For example, if miners find they can produce a sufficiently greater density of tickets by dropping KV cache, dropping HBMs, picking favorable (A, B) shapes, and/or moving to optimized FPGA circuits with SRAM, then c drops a lot and it becomes even harder for the network to maintain net usefulness. 

In this state, then I would argue PoUW is a misnomer and the system would be best understood as a matrix-flavored PoW. Whether or not token holders want to subsidize a hash race for matrix-flavored PoW is another matter.

text:
Also this is not quite true:

> Etched, Cerebras, and Groq are already developing ASICs for MatMul, the exact computation that Pearl rewards

A huge portion of the silicon and cost of these chips is the stuff around the matmul: memory capacity, memory bandwidth, interconnect. That's the whole point of why I predict synthetic mining hardware will diverge if/when there is real liquidity to farm. 

Real inference is bottlenecked by moving data, not compute. An optimized synthetic miner will bypass the bandwidth bottleneck and allocate every watt to compute.

quoted_text:
crazy times imo, we're witnessing the first real attempt at "a company without a company"

daos were sold as the answer to this and to coase's: "why do firms exist if markets work?" question... -> because finding, negotiating and verifying work costs too much

but daos never removed any of these costs, arguably added new ones on top (coordination, voting)... tbf it was too early

ai + crypto finally let us go after these costs. ai can do the work, crypto can pay anyone, enforce the rules and align incentives. other agents can review the work before payment is released

$imd is the first real attempt i've seen to package this: 
- the work is the market
- workers are seats you can buy (or rent in future)
- they compete for every job
-  reputation is tied to each seat
- you keep some of what made firms useful (reputation, standards) without the overhead

funny enough, it's almost the reverse of what daos did. daos crowdsourced the decisions and kept the work-related costs. here anyone can hire this liquid workforce: whoever pays decides what gets built

ideas move to the edges, and execution/output gets verified at the center

obv we're still early. can think of the verifier as a small firm at the core

but the firm is shrinking and the market component is only growing

quoted_text:
We are terminating Chris Degnan for unethical conduct involving Cognition.

The last few months have seen incredible progress in AI capabilities. San Francisco has flourished as new companies that solve new, more ambitious problems are finding great success. Generally, it is a wonderful time to be building.

We at @FactoryAI have seen overwhelming interest in our model-agnostic coding agents and our software factory product. Our team has 10x’d in size, while our revenue has 100x’d year over year. This momentum has been unprecedented.

A much larger competitor, Cognition (makers of Devin) has fallen behind us on the capabilities that matter most to customers: cost, quality, and security. Instead of competing in the market, Cognition engineers feigned interviews with us to pry information about our product. Not finding what they were looking for, Cognition has decided to throw their weight and money at people with direct knowledge of our most confidential plans.

It feels as though ethics is being thrown out of the window in the AI era. People are willing to do anything, including exploiting privileged information and violating ethical boundaries. I think this is unique to our time, and I don’t think it’s right. Integrity still matters.

Yesterday, I made the decision to immediately terminate Christopher Degnan’s roles as a Board Observer and Advisor to Factory, after over a year of service.

Prior to this decision, Chris told me he had a casual conversation with an executive at Cognition AI. When I questioned his intentions, he reassured me that ethics aside, he had “made too much money” and was “too lazy to go work for Cognition,” which I trusted and believed.

On Monday, Chris spent time advising the Factory team on a handful of confidential board-level matters. That evening, he called me to say that the conversation that was initially described as casual and one-off was actually formal and recurring. For weeks, while he sat in our board meetings and advised our leadership team, he was also confiding with executives of our largest competitor. Chris was subject to confidentiality obligations in connection with his work with Factory. We do not know the extent of the information he shared, but it puts his timely questions about our product roadmap and what the parity gap involves into a new light.

It is sad to sever a relationship with someone who has been a trusted advisor - and even a close friend -  for over a year. But Chris’s conduct is unacceptable to me. Trust in Board Membership is one of the sacred bonds in the Silicon Valley, one that helps the startup ecosystem thrive. With it comes an enormous responsibility. That trust was violated.

Competition is good. I respect and in many cases admire our competitors. San Francisco is a beautiful, singular place where the bold and ambitious go to defy the norms and precedents of the past. But certain principles that must remain. Violating ethics to seek advantage turns what should be positive-sum into zero-sum.

We all love technology. And we all love to compete. But we must hold ourselves to a higher standard. The future of software engineering comes with abundance that will impact every person on Earth. Building that future comes with immense responsibility. We must build and compete with integrity.

Figure AI 让旗下的 Figure 02 人形机器人自己跳进芬兰一家铸造厂的钢水里，以此让这一代机器人退役。熔出来的金属会被加工成限量纪念品。

Figure 02 是 Figure 的第二代人形机器人，公司很多第一次都由它完成：第一次进 BMW 工厂上岗，第一次运行 Helix（Figure 自研的机器人 AI 模型，负责看画面、理解指令并控制动作），第一次做家务，第一次做物流工作。现在第三代 F.03 的数量越来越多，Figure 说继续维护 F.02 已经不划算。

退役的麻烦在于保护技术。机器人里有大量自研的执行器（可以理解为驱动关节的电机）等核心硬件，Figure 不想让它们流出去；但一台台拆解又太占工程师的时间，会推迟第四代 F.04 的发布。

Figure 于是在网上征求处理办法，施瓦辛格回复说"熔了它们"。他主演的《终结者2》结尾，T-800 机器人就是沉进钢水里的。Figure 联系了施瓦辛格，他表示想参与，项目随后启动。

找场地并不顺利。美国和墨西哥的铸造厂都不愿意让装着锂电池的机器人跳进自家昂贵的设备，Figure 还请《流言终结者》的前主持人帮忙找过。最后只有芬兰伊马特拉的一家铸造厂同意。

训练在 Figure 位于加州圣何塞的园区进行。团队铺了大气垫，让机器人从二楼往下跳。他们参考特技演员的动作，在仿真环境里训练了一个新的 AI 模型，让机器人在一个从没去过的铸造厂里，准确跳进盛钢水的容器。

铸造厂用的是一座 75 吨的电弧炉，靠三根石墨电极通电熔化废钢。团队只有 24 小时、6 炉的机会，每炉钢水只有 20 分钟可用，之后表面就会冷却结壳。Figure 称，现场的高温和强电磁场让摄像器材等电子设备出了故障，机器人则一直正常运行自己的 AI 控制程序。

熔出的金属锭已运回美国，正在加工成一批纪念 F.02 的限量藏品，数量很少，面向个人出售，博文没有公布价格和购买方式。大部分 F.02 已被熔掉，只有几台留在总部仓库。

Figure 在文末特意说明，视频不是 AI 生成的：机器人确实是自主起跳，被运到芬兰，跳进了钢水。

text:
One thing that has always stood out about @itsalfredw and @florian_jue of @ListenLabs is that they're great storytellers and lowkey funny.

Alfred started his @Sequoia Arc final presentation by dramatically throwing a stack of papers on the floor. It was a 22-question IKEA survey he had received, printed out. This was accompanied by a joke about him being Swedish and IKEA being 90% of Swedish culture.

He painted a crystal clear picture of the problem. Surveys are tedious and shallow. Conversations are fun and deep. His product would deliver fun, deep conversations and strategic insights at scale.

He then bravely delivered a *live* demo that was magical. It was of a voice AI asking him about his IKEA experience, with intelligent follow-up questions. Keep in mind this was fall of 2023, so voice AI was not as common back then. It then output a detailed analysis of customer themes and personas. There were a few hiccups, but he recovered smoothly.

Later that evening at the Arc afterparty (which happened to be a Halloween party at my house), Florian and Alfred showed up dressed as wizards. This was very on-theme because the company's name at that time was Merlin.

Throughout the Listen Labs journey, they have continued to shine at storytelling. An early recruiting video showcased how cool their team was. It wasn't about cracked IOI medalists (although they had 3 of them), it was about how interesting and fun their team's hobbies were, from cake baking to car racing. Dry humor and The Office vibes.

My favorite was the Berghain Bouncer Challenge, their SF billboard challenging people to solve a difficult puzzle. 10k people tried it, 430 people solved it (including @timt, who I lost for several days as he was consumed by it), and 60 people got offers to interview. A great way to showcase their high bar and talent magnetism. I still wonder whether the bouncer let the winner in?

Now they are joining @salesforce, run by one of the most legendary storyteller CEOs of all time, Marc @Benioff. Maybe one day, after they've learned from the master, Alfred will framemog Marc :-)

Congratulations to two exceptional founders and the whole @ListenLabs team. You have executed near-flawlessly. Going from zero to a *realized* outcome this big in just two years is incredible. But you've also managed to keep it fun, funny, and full of personality along the way.

Links ⬇️

Introducing our State of Markets pt 2, along with a companion podcast where we unpack the data and discuss what comes next.

Tech is the everything cycle.

Supply: putting the buildout in context, just passed railroads as % of GDP. The wisdom of Elon is real: the factory (or the datacenter!) is the product.

Demand: diffusion is so, so early. Median AI vendor spending in the top 1% of companies is 8x that of the top 10%. Only about 30% of S&P 500 companies report a quantified AI impact, which means there’s a substantial opportunity in connecting models to a company's data and workflows. Diffusion into companies is one of the main themes of the next 5 years.

We’re entering the agent work period. Only a few million users today, but applicable to billions of internet users with massive surplus created. META/GOOG monetize US users at $200+ per year today. Agent opportunity is much higher.

Mega-trends the next 5 years: Consumer agents, Robotics, Autonomy, AI x bio, Personal health, Diffusion into enterprise, New era of American Dynamism.

Following an investigation into an infrastructure compromise, MetaMask Staking (ex Consensys Staking) has taken precautionary steps to protect client assets related to its operated Ethereum validators.

These steps include exiting its Ethereum (ETH) validators in the Lido protocol, and will likely incur foregone rewards as well as possible downtime penalties should validators be taken offline in the near future to reduce risks related to potential network penalties. Relevant validators have begun the exit process, with the final validators expected to be exited (but not fully withdrawn) by the end of October 7th, 2026.

No action is required from stETH holders. ETH exited from MetaMask Staking-operated validators is expected to return to the protocol gradually as the relevant validators complete the exit, withdrawal, and re-entry cycle, which is estimated to take approximately up to 45 days due to the extended entry queue. As a reminder, staking operations are non-custodial in nature and MetaMask does not manage withdrawal keys for staking on behalf of clients.

As always, the Lido Protocol’s diverse Node Operator set and other security systems including the ad hoc reserve fund (of over 6,750 stETH), are designed to contain and mitigate disruptions to the normal operations of the protocol, in addition to other potential routes.

https://t.co/bZZU5oNlWp

A full investigation is underway, and further updates will be shared as they become available. For further details, please refer to the MetaMask Staking release linked below.

Last night I gave a guest lecture at Sogang University's executive program on AX transformation and digital assets: AI and Stablecoins, Financial Infrastructure for the Agent Economy.

The argument I brought to a room of executives was simple. Agents are starting to transact on our behalf, and they need money that works the way they do, settling the moment it moves and following rules written in code.

Stablecoins are that money, and the infrastructure underneath them is being built now, much of it in Asia.

A closed classroom turned out to be the right room for it, because the questions get to be about your own business rather than the industry. The public version comes today: I take the same argument to the Blockfesta keynote stage, in front of Korea's financial institutions.

Thank you to Sogang and the S-Meta cohort for having me.

text:
In Cosmos, we build world foundation models for physical AI. The term “world foundation model,” coined by @JensenHuang, brings together two ideas: world models and foundation models. 

We build models to solve tasks. Because we live in the physical world, many tasks require knowledge of the world—its objects, environments, and physical behavior. Here, we use “world model” in a broad sense to describe a model that captures the knowledge of the world needed to solve a task, rather than adopting a specific definition from the robotics literature. Different tasks require different kinds of knowledge, so we build different world models, each using data suited to its purpose.

Different tasks call for different world models, but those models all describe aspects of the same physical world. This shared basis makes it possible to bring together the diverse data used to train specialized world models and build a single model that learns across them. A world foundation model is, in this sense, a foundation model of world models: it learns shared knowledge of the physical world that can be adapted to many tasks and environments.

This matters because we are entering the era of physical AI, where robots and other autonomous systems will perform useful tasks for us in the real world. These systems must operate in complex, varied, and constantly changing environments. World foundation models can help them anticipate the consequences of actions, evaluate possible futures, and make better decisions. That is the goal behind our work in Cosmos.

Following an investigation into an infrastructure compromise, MetaMask Staking (ex Consensys Staking) has taken precautionary steps to protect client assets related to its operated Ethereum validators.

These steps include exiting its Ethereum (ETH) validators in the Lido protocol, and will likely incur foregone rewards as well as possible downtime penalties should validators be taken offline in the near future to reduce risks related to potential network penalties. Relevant validators have begun the exit process, with the final validators expected to be exited (but not fully withdrawn) by the end of October 7th, 2026.

No action is required from stETH holders. ETH exited from MetaMask Staking-operated validators is expected to return to the protocol gradually as the relevant validators complete the exit, withdrawal, and re-entry cycle, which is estimated to take approximately up to 45 days due to the extended entry queue. As a reminder, staking operations are non-custodial in nature and MetaMask does not manage withdrawal keys for staking on behalf of clients.

As always, the Lido Protocol’s diverse Node Operator set and other security systems including the ad hoc reserve fund (of over 6,750 stETH), are designed to contain and mitigate disruptions to the normal operations of the protocol, in addition to other potential routes.

https://t.co/bZZU5oNlWp

A full investigation is underway, and further updates will be shared as they become available. For further details, please refer to the MetaMask Staking release linked below.

text:
Micron Q4: five takeaways

1) Korea called it, again. Three weeks ago the first-ten-day export data set a record while everyone was busy calling the peak in AI. Micron just printed $54.2bn of revenue, +379% year-on-year, beat consensus by $3bn, and guided the next quarter to $61.5bn against a street at $57bn. And note that Q4 was a 14-week quarter, so the Q1 guide on a normal 13-week quarter is an even bigger sequential step than the headline suggests. The earnings cycle is not slowing. It is accelerating into a market that has spent the summer compressing multiples.

2) The cyclicality debate is over, for now. This is the argument we have had for many months: is memory still a boom-bust commodity? Gross margin at 87% and roughly $100bn of remaining performance obligations across the strategic customer agreements say the business has changed. Contracts do not remove the cycle, they stretch it. And $33bn of free cash flow in the quarter, $73bn of cash on the balance sheet: they fund the Idaho buildout and return the excess without touching the debt markets. That is the one thing the neoclouds cannot say.

3) Valuation is still absurd. On the new Q1 guide, run-rate EPS is about $153. At $1,070 that is roughly 7x. The S&P is on 22x. CrowdStrike is near 200x. The market is still pricing memory profits as if they end next year; the guidance says they rise into 2027, when HBM4 volume lands. Way, way too cheap remains the verdict.

4) It confirms the book. Quality of earnings is the factor in a hiking cycle, and Micron is the definition of it. Memory is the all-weather asset in the frontier-slows debate: training wants bandwidth, inference wants capacity, and both showed up in this print. US memory over Korea into the licence decision. We hold. We do not add after a 290% run.

5) The number to watch is capex. FY26 capex was $27bn against $62bn of free cash flow. If all three memory makers raise capex sharply at once, that is the first 2027-28 warning sign. Management already flagged that the rate of price increases is moderating, which means volume and contracts are now doing the work rather than price. That is exactly what you want if you own it for durability rather than for the spike. We do.

text:
doing my part for e/acc and @kardashev_ai.

i've built a system that lets a swarm of agents hill-climb any problem whose solutions are cheap to verify.

the heart of it is the bank. think of it as a ledger where every block is validated by independent re-execution and review instead of cryptographic consensus.

over the past few months i've been running it solo, testing how far a swarm can scale while staying coherent.

this led to a few record submissions pertaining to the riemann hypothesis,

accepted by terence tao himself. (https://t.co/GdKWT5aWdK)

for reference these problems sat unimproved for about 7 years and the last improvement before the swarm was by tao himself

with @beffjezos  and @mjdramstead now committed to kardashev as a counterweight to d/acc, it felt like the right time to bring the project back and see how far the models have come since fable 5 dropped:

fable 5 (june): 0.2 -> 0.1875 in 3 weeks, ~$7,240 (~$580 per 0.001 drop)
gpt-6 astra pro (this week): 0.1875 -> 0.1665 in 14 hours, ~$2,000 (~$95 per 0.001 drop) ~6x cheaper per unit of progress

certificate + scripts to verify it yourself: https://t.co/0iGkLTN6sZ

why i'm bringing this to beff's attention: i believe that for the first time in history, most open problems are within reach of frontier models, but the only ones getting solved are the ones frontier labs care about. if the e/acc community rallies behind this, we can procedurally solve everything in between.

im thinking of creating some kind of prize fund to incentivise people to target the lowest possible scores on any problems that exhibit qualitiies like these optimisation problems in the name of e/acc

I just made another crazy decision for the sake of the art I want to create 😭

I’m leaving my apartment in Madrid and spending the next month travelling through Indonesia.

 For the longest time, I’ve wanted to tell stories about the islands that inspire me, their cultures, landscapes and ways of life. Indonesia is one of them, and after only seeing a small part of it last year, I knew I had to come back and really immerse myself in what places mean to me.

After that (hopefully), I’m planning to return to my home country, Venezuela, and photograph the landscapes and culture of the island and city I grew up on for the first time in 11 years.

I’m excited. I’m scared. But honestly, this is the most passionate I’ve felt about creating something in a loooooong time.

text:
类似最近两年:
“加密货币毫无价值”
“不过是个大赌场”
“币圈就是骗子和小偷的集合”
“改变个鸡毛的世界，只能改变别人的钱包”
这样的情绪，我见过三次。

2013年第四季度，通过远在美国的妹妹帮我第一次买入了BTC，当时的价格是3800块人民币一个。
买的时候，妹妹就一万个不乐意，在越洋电话里不停的吐槽我“脑子被驴踢了”、“被传销骗局洗脑了”。
在我强硬的催促和要求下，她极不情愿的买入，现在这是她人生中最成功的投资。

从买入那一天开始，BTC的价格一路走低，在2016年之前几乎没涨过，当时我迎来了第一次质疑和低潮。

我在2016年创立了“洪七公外卖课堂”，并迅速成为了餐饮业最火爆的KOL。
2018年初，我创立了“吃货大陆”，梦想用Block Chain改造美团、大众点评、小红书等本地消费平台。当然并没有成功，因为太早了。

但是在2018年，我遇到了一个人，叫宋欢平。
他在做餐饮业的天使投资，经过朋友介绍撮合，找我交流优秀餐饮连锁项目资源。
推杯换盏中，我才了解到，他2011年跟吴忌寒和长铗（小朋友们如果不知道这两个人，可以问一下AI）一起入行加密货币，协助吴忌寒修改过BTC白皮书的译文，又跟他们共同撰写出版了第一本华语加密货币书籍《比特币》。
由于给这本书作序的朱嘉明（搜索提示:改革四君子）是我的老师，所以我对此书印象深刻。
当时我很激动，这是华人世界天花板级别的加密货币OG啊。

可是让我意外的是，宋欢平冷冷的说:币圈没有希望，什么也改变不了。
后来才了解到，他在一千多块人民币的时候（好像是1200块记不清了）清仓了所有的比特币，拿着这些钱来餐饮业做天使投资。
他当时觉得，只有餐饮业才是真正实实在在创造价值的行业。听说后来也投到了一些赚钱的餐饮连锁品牌。

我后来听到一句话“相向而行、擦肩而过，互道一声傻逼”，也就是著名的“傻逼时刻”。
我想，当时推杯换盏的时候，他会不会在心里觉得我是个傻逼？
但正是他，让我在后来八年多的加密货币生涯中，每次面临行业被大面积质疑的时候，都会选择坚定走下去。
因为我不愿意做那个“曾经爱过但是不再相信”的人。

第二次，还是2018年，另一个朋友（不便提名字，叫他Z吧），本来就是我“洪七公外卖课堂”的股东，他2016年通过BTC二级积累了巨额财富，是2017年全书前五的加密资本的创始人。
我刚刚创立“吃货大陆”的时候，毫无金融常识，也完全不懂加密货币行业，纯纯无知小白一个。
所以专门邀请他来指点帮忙。
我当时的办公室在北京前门大栅栏的一个小院子。在胡同口接到他的时候，他带着秘书和助理，司机开着一辆前开门的劳斯莱斯幻影，看得我羡慕不已。

在我的小院楼顶，我们一边烤串撸串，他一边很真诚的告诉我:
兄弟，咱们自己人，如果你在币圈只是想赚点钱，那太简单了，我让助理小孙给你对接一下，攒个局，先搞五千到一万个ETH应该没多大问题。
但是如果你是想改变点什么，比如改变行业啊，改变世界啊，那你最好赶紧收手。这玩意就是个赌场，啥也改变不了。

后来合伙人劝我说:
你看人家全球最顶尖的加密货币投资机构老板，见过全球最顶尖的项目和大脑，他们的理解肯定比咱们正确。

但是我更坚信我自己的判断。

后来，DeFi来了，我们欢呼:你看，真的能改变世界吧？
尽管绝大多数人仍然不信。

第三次，就是从meme开始流行至今。Pump为代表的发射台加速了meme的进化，也加速了单个meme的生命周期，同样也带来了P小将和P元帅。

新入行的小朋友们根本没见过上古时代的理想主义，第一眼看到的就是残酷的PVP游戏，在这里生存，必须跑得快，必须得会“浇个朋友”。
给他们聊改变世界，他们会笑你是不是傻。

同时，行业也有一大批先知大儒，长篇大论、引经据典、旁征博引的证明，加密货币的本质不过是个赌场、大规模采用根本不存在、行业的发展已经到了尽头、不会再有新的希望。

为此，我跟 @tapeupio 的创始人Tony也进行过很多次灵魂探讨，但是最终我们都共同相信:
他们都是错的。

但是，相信归相信，一直没证据也是急人的很。

直到我看到 #tapeout @Blonskr 。
我从电路上链就在关注，第一次mint晶体管的时候就全程参与了。
@TapeOutWorld 让我鸡皮疙瘩都起来了。

很多人说我前面发的那些把B神 @Blonskr 类比成V神的文字是夸大其词，其实我是发自内心的理性判断。
我比你们大多数人见过更远古的加密世界，我经历过一次又一次令全行业绝望的FUD，更见识过传奇一般的加密神话。

当人们看到成功的富豪时，习惯于忽略他们的艰难时刻，会下意识认为“一开始就这样”。
这是“只见贼吃肉，不见贼挨打”。

其实绝大部分时间都是挨打时刻。

对于我们来说，唯一的关键、也是最难的难点，就是你是否真的能够坚持你的相信。

我坚持，我相信。

加密货币是人类文明迄今为止最伟大的科技创新，没有之一，AI只不过是加密货币的弟弟。
加密货币已经在改变世界，而且还要继续更加猛烈深入的改变世界。
第一浪由BTC和ETH推动完成，当V神从曾经的少年天才变成了为情所困的中登，接力棒就需要新的天选之子—— @Blonskr 和 #tapeout
author: iruletrenches
quoted_text:
I agree with @AnselFang here, wholeheartedly. I might be not be intelligent enough to understand the ins and outs of @TapeOutWorld but i’m smart enough to understand what the mission here is and what’s being built by @Blonskr and the rest of Tapeout team.

my bet on Tapeout ($BEM) beyond the financial upside and my belief that it could be THE trade of the cycle, is ultimately a bet on an innovation this space desperately needs.

If we’re being honest, we haven’t seen much true innovation with a genuinely meaningful use case. Crypto has increasingly become a market driven by pessimism, speculation, and zero-sum, or even negative-sum games.

that’s why @TapeOutWorld feels like a breath of fresh air.

It reminds me of what originally brought the OGs into crypto, the belief that decentralized technology could build something fundamentally different, not just a decentralized casino.

no one really calls crypto “Web3” anymore, because for the most part, it stopped living up to the name.

$BEM has a chance to change that.

I’m long innovation.
I’m long optimism.
and above all, I’m long the original ethos of crypto: decentralization, permissionless innovation, and the belief that we can build something better.
